prompt: What do you know about Supabase?
answer:
is an  open-source backend -as-a-service  (BaaS)  platform  built around  PostgreSQL . It’s often described  as an open -source alternative to  Firebase,  but it gives  you much more  direct access to  a traditional relational  database.
What Supabase provides
• PostgreSQL database  — a full Postgres  database, with SQL , relationships, extensions , indexes, functions, triggers , and more.
• Authentication  — email/password, magic  links, OAuth providers , phone auth, and  other  authentication flows.
• Auto-generated APIs  — REST APIs (and  other tooling) generated  from your database  schema.
• Realtime  — subscribe to database  changes and broadcast  messages to connected  clients.
• Storage  — object/file storage  for images,  videos, documents, etc ., with access policies .
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript  functions running close  to users .
• Row Level Security  (RLS)  — PostgreSQL's security  system can be  used to control  exactly  which rows each  user can access .
• Dashboard and developer  tooling  — SQL editor, database  management, logs, authentication  management , storage management, etc .
Why developers like  it
The big appeal  is that  your backend is  fundamentally Postgres , rather than an  opaque proprietary database  abstraction.

You can start  extremely quickly:

prompt: What do you know about https://supabase.com/?
answer:
is essentially a  backend-as-a-service built around PostgreSQL . It gives you a database plus many of the backend services you normally have to build yourself.
What Supabase gives you
• PostgreSQL database  — Every project gets a full Postgres database rather than a proprietary database abstraction. You can use normal SQL, indexes, functions, triggers, extensions, etc.
• Authentication  — Email/password, passwordless login, OAuth and other identity options.
• Row Level Security (RLS)  — A particularly important feature. You can put authorization rules directly on database tables, e.g. "users can only read their own records."
• Storage  — Upload and serve images, videos, documents and other files, with access controlled through policies.
• Realtime  — Subscribe to database changes and synchronize state between clients. Useful for chat, collaborative apps, dashboards, multiplayer features, etc.
• Edge Functions  — Server-side TypeScript functions running on Supabase's edge infrastructure. They're useful for webhooks, API endpoints, integrations, AI calls and business logic that shouldn't run in the browser.
• APIs  — Supabase automatically provides APIs around your database, so a frontend can interact with Postgres without you having to build a conventional CRUD API for everything.
• Vector/AI functionality  — PostgreSQL extensions such as  pgvector  can be used for embeddings and similarity search.
• Cron and queues  — Supabase has also expanded beyond the basic "Firebase alternative" model into scheduled jobs and queues.
Why developers like it
The big attraction is  how much backend you get without assembling 6–10 separate services .
For example, imagine you're building a SaaS application:
React / Next.js frontend
You can get surprisingly far without running your own backend server.
And because the underlying database is  actual PostgreSQL , you're not learning an entirely proprietary database model. That's one of Supabase's biggest differentiators from something like Firebase.
Supabase vs. Firebase

If you're comfortable with SQL and relational data,  Supabase is often a very natural choice .
The really interesting part: RLS
I'd pay particular attention to  Row Level Security  if you're considering Supabase.
Instead of having your backend constantly do:
Who is this user?
you can encode authorization into PostgreSQL itself:
User
For example, conceptually:
create policy "Users can view their own profiles"
That can make architectures dramatically simpler—but  bad RLS policies can also create serious security vulnerabilities , so this is an area where you need to understand what you're doing. Supabase itself specifically recommends RLS for protecting tables exposed through its APIs.
Is it actually "serverless"?
Sort of.
You don't need to manage traditional application servers for many applications, but underneath it you're still dealing with substantial infrastructure: PostgreSQL, connection pooling, functions, storage, networking, etc.
Supabase manages that infrastructure for you.
And if you want more control, Supabase emphasizes its open-source architecture and supports self-hosting.
Where I think Supabase shines
I'd seriously consider it for:
• SaaS applications
• Internal tools
• Marketplaces
• Mobile apps
• Dashboards
• AI applications
• CRUD-heavy applications
• Multi-user applications
• Apps needing authentication + database + file storage
• Prototypes that may eventually become production systems
It's particularly attractive for  small teams and startups , because one developer can build a substantial backend very quickly.
Supabase itself now explicitly positions the platform for AI applications and "AI builders," and its ecosystem includes integrations with things like OpenAI, Stripe and other third-party services.
One important caveat
I wouldn't think of Supabase as "just a database."
Its biggest architectural advantage is really:
Postgres + Auth + authorization + APIs + storage + realtime + server-side functions, all designed to work together.
That's what makes it compelling.
If you're evaluating Supabase for a  specific project , tell me what you're building and what stack you're using (e.g. React/Next.js, Python, Flutter, mobile, AI agent, etc.). I can then tell you  exactly how I'd architect it with Supabase, including the database schema, RLS, authentication, APIs and what should/shouldn't live in Edge Functions.

prompt: What do you know about https://supabase.com/?
answer:
is essentially a  backend-as-a-service platform built around PostgreSQL . If you're building a web or mobile app, it can provide much of the backend infrastructure you'd otherwise have to assemble yourself.
What Supabase gives you
• PostgreSQL database  — A real  Postgres database, not a proprietary database abstraction. You get SQL, relationships, indexes, extensions, functions, triggers, etc.
• Authentication  — Email/password, passwordless login,  OAuth/social providers, JWTs, and integration with your database's security policies.
• Row Level Security (RLS)  — One of its most important features. You can define database  policies such as "users can only read their own records," allowing your application to interact with the database relatively directly while retaining fine-grained authorization.
• Auto-generated APIs  — Your Postgres schema can be exposed through APIs, so you don't necessarily need to write a conventional CRUD backend for every table.
• Storage  — Object/file storage for things like images, videos, documents , and user uploads, with access controlled through policies.
• Realtime  — Clients can subscribe to database changes and communicate through realtime channels , useful for chat, collaborative apps, dashboards, multiplayer features, etc.
• Edge Functions  — Server-side TypeScript/Deno functions for things that shouldn't run in the browser—web hooks, payments, integrations, AI calls, custom APIs, and so on.
• Vector/AI capabilities  — Support for  vector embeddings and Postgres extensions such as  pgvector , which makes it useful for RAG and AI applications.
• Local development and self-hosting  — Supabase is open source and provides tooling for running much of the stack locally.
The interesting part
The architecture is roughly:
Your Web / Mobile App
The big differentiator is that  Postgres is the center of everything . Supabase explicitly says it doesn't abstract the database away—you get a full PostgreSQL database, with Auth, Storage, Realtime and other services built around it.
Supabase vs. Firebase
A useful mental model is:
Supabase ≈ Firebase, but PostgreSQL-first rather than Google/NoSQL-first.

Where I'd consider using it
Supabase is particularly attractive for:
• SaaS products
• Admin dashboards
• Mobile apps
• Marketplaces
• Internal business applications
• MVPs/startups
• AI/RAG applications

• Real-time applications

It can dramatically reduce the amount of infrastructure code you need to write. Supabase itself currently positions the platform around going from a new project to a production backend quickly, while retaining the underlying Postgres database.
One thing I'd be careful about
RLS is extremely powerful, but you need to understand it properly.  A poorly designed RLS policy can result in either users being unable to access data they should see—or, much worse, users accessing data they shouldn't. Supabase's architecture makes database authorization a central part of application security.
So I wouldn't think of Supabase as simply "a database with a nice UI." It's closer to  a complete application backend whose foundation happens to be PostgreSQL .

• Auto-generated APIs  — Your database can  be accessed through  generated REST APIs  and client libraries , with GraphQL also  available.
• Storage  — Object/file storage  for things like  images, videos and  documents, integrated with  Postgres/RLS.

• Edge Functions  — Server-side TypeScript /Deno functions for  things such  as  webhooks, payments, API  endpoints and integrations .
• Vector/AI functionality  — It supports storing  and searching vector  embeddings, alongside the  rest of your  Postgres data.
• Developer tooling  — Dashboard, SQL editor , CLI, local development , migrations, APIs and  SDKs for JavaScript /TypeScript,  Python, Flutter , Swift, C#, Kotlin  and others.
The important architectural  idea
The big distinction  from something like  Firebase is that Postgres is the  center of the  system .

This is particularly  powerful because  RLS lets you  put authorization rules  close to the  data . For example, you  can have a documents  table and tell  Postgres that a  user may only  read rows where documents.owner_id = auth.uid() . Supabase's Data API  is designed to  work with this  model.
Why developers like  it
The appeal is  that you can  go from:
"I have an  idea for an  app"
to:
"I have a database, user accounts, APIs , file storage and  realtime functionality"
without provisioning servers  and wiring together  five different SaaS  products.

prompt: What do you know about Supabase (@supabase on X/Twitter)?
answer:
is a developer -focused backend platform built around  PostgreSQL . Its pitch is essentially:  give developers a powerful Postgres database, then provide the backend infrastructure you typically have to build around it.
What Supabase actually provides
The core stack includes:
• Postgres database  — each project gets a real PostgreSQL database, rather than a proprietary database abstraction.
• Authentication  — email/password , social login, MFA, and authorization through Postgres Row Level Security.
• Storage  — object/file storage for things like images, videos, and documents.
• Realtime  — subscribe to database changes and build multiplayer /live applications.
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript/JavaScript functions running on Deno, useful for APIs, webhooks, payments,  AI calls, etc.
• Auto-generated APIs  — APIs are exposed from your database so you can interact with Postgres without building every  CRUD endpoint yourself.
• Vector/AI capabilities  — Postgres can store and search embeddings, making it useful for RAG and AI applications.
• Dashboard and developer tooling  — SQL  editor, table editor, logs, database management, migrations, etc.
So a typical application might look like:
React / Next.js → Supabase API → Postgres ↘ Auth ↘ Storage ↘ Realtime ↘ Edge Functions
That integration is the important part: the pieces aren't independent SaaS products bolted together; they're designed around the same Postgres database.
Why developers like it
The big advantage is  speed without giving up SQL/Postgres .
Instead of assembling:
AWS RDS + authentication provider + S3 + API server + WebSocket infrastructure + database permissions + monitoring
you can get a large portion of that from one platform.
It is particularly attractive for:
• SaaS startups
• MVPs
• internal tools
• dashboards
• marketplaces
• mobile apps
• AI applications
• applications where relational data matters
• developers who prefer SQL/Postgres over Firebase's document-oriented model
And unlike some "backend as a service" products,  your underlying database is standard Postgres . That's a significant architectural selling point.
Supabase vs. Firebase
This is probably the most useful comparison.

Supabase's strategy is basically  "Firebase, but built around Postgres."
Pricing
As of September 2026, Supabase has a  $0 Free plan , with 500 MB database storage, 1 GB file storage, 50,000 monthly active users, 2 million  Realtime messages, and 500,000 Edge Function invocations. The Pro plan starts at  $25/month , with additional usage-based charges.
One thing I'd pay attention to at scale is that Supabase isn't simply "one flat $25 server." Compute, egress, storage,  database size, Realtime usage, etc. can contribute to the bill.
And @supabase on X?
The  @supabase  account is essentially the company's developer-facing social presence. Supabase has built a fairly strong developer brand around open source, Postgres, modern web development, AI tooling, and its rapidly expanding  platform.
The interesting thing about Supabase isn't really its individual features—most of them have competitors.  Its strategic bet is that Postgres becomes the default foundation for modern application backends, while Supabase becomes the easiest way to build around it.
If you're asking because you're evaluating  Supabase as a company/investment, considering using it for a project, or trying to understand what @supabase is doing on X , I can go much deeper into any of those angles.

answer:
Yes. I’d describe  Supabase  as one of the most important developer platforms in the modern “build an app quickly” ecosystem.
is essentially a  Postgres-centered backend platform : instead of assembling a database, authentication system, file storage, APIs, realtime infrastructure, and serverless functions separately, you can get them as an integrated platform.
What Supabase actually is
The core idea is important:  Supabase is not its own proprietary database. It's built around PostgreSQL.
Every Supabase project gets a full Postgres database, with direct database access rather than an abstraction hiding Postgres from you. Around that database Supabase provides:
• Postgres database  — full SQL/Postgres , extensions, indexes, transactions , etc.
• Authentication  — email/password, social  login and user  management.
• Row Level Security  (RLS)  — database-level policies  controlling who can  access which rows .
• Data APIs  — REST APIs generated  from your database  schema.
• Realtime  — subscriptions to database  changes and realtime  functionality.
• Storage  — files such as  images, videos and  documents.
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript /Deno functions.
• Vector/AI capabilities  — including support for  embeddings and Postgres  extensions such as pgvector .
• Dashboard, CLI, migrations  and local development  tooling.
That architecture is a big part of its appeal. You can start with essentially:
React/Next.js → Supabase → Postgres
rather than building a conventional backend/API/database stack yourself.
Its REST API can even be generated directly from your Postgres schema, so tables and relationships become accessible through an API without you having to write a conventional CRUD backend.
Why developers like it
The killer combination is  Postgres + developer experience .
If you're already comfortable with SQL, you aren't learning some proprietary database model. And if you're  not  comfortable with Postgres, Supabase gives you a UI and APIs that make it relatively approachable. Supabase explicitly positions itself as making Postgres easier to use rather than replacing it.
There's also a major  open-source  component. Supabase says its architecture is open source and is built largely from existing open-source projects rather than reinventing every component.

prompt: What do you know about Supabase (https://supabase.com/, @supabase on X/Twitter)?
answer:
is a  Postgres-centered backend platform  designed to give developers most of what they need to build  and run a modern web or mobile application without assembling a backend from scratch.
What it actually provides
The key distinction is that Supabase isn't simply a hosted database. Each project gives you a  real PostgreSQL database , with a set of services built around it.
• Postgres  — full PostgreSQL, including SQL, extensions, indexes, JSON, relational constraints , etc.
• Auth  — email/password, magic links, OTP, OAuth/social login, SSO and MFA. Authentication integrates directly with Postgres and Row Level Security (RLS).
• Data APIs  — automatically generated APIs for interacting with your database.
• Storage  — object/file storage for images, videos, documents, etc., with  authorization tied into Postgres /RLS.
• Realtime  — subscribe to database changes and build collaborative /live applications.
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript/Deno functions for things like webhooks, APIs, payments and AI orchestration.
• Vector/AI capabilities  — storage, indexing and querying of vector embeddings, alongside Postgres.
• Cron and Queues  — increasingly, it can handle background/scheduled workloads as well.
The architecture is roughly:
Your application
That's one of its biggest advantages:  your application data, authentication, authorization and backend logic can all revolve around PostgreSQL , rather than having a separate database + auth provider + file store + realtime system that you have to glue together.
Why developers like it
The developer experience is probably Supabase's biggest selling point.
For example, you can create a Postgres table, turn on RLS, create an auth flow, and query the database from a React/Next.js application with relatively little infrastructure code. Supabase provides client libraries for JavaScript, Python, Flutter and other environments.
It is also  open source and self-hostable , and the underlying database is standard PostgreSQL rather than a proprietary database abstraction. Supabase explicitly emphasizes portability and says you can migrate data to and from other PostgreSQL databases.
That makes it quite different philosophically from something like Firebase.

If you already think naturally in  SQL, tables, relationships, joins, constraints and transactions , Supabase is particularly attractive.
It's become particularly interesting for AI applications
This is an area where Supabase has become much more than "Firebase but with Postgres."
Postgres can store application data  and vector embeddings , allowing an AI application to keep things such as:
users
in the same underlying database.
That makes architectures such as  RAG applications, AI agents, SaaS products and AI-generated applications  relatively straightforward.
Supabase is also explicitly targeting AI builders, and its current platform includes vector capabilities, Edge Functions and tooling for AI workloads.
Another interesting development: "Supabase for Platforms"
Supabase has also moved beyond simply being something an individual developer signs up for.
Its  Supabase for Platforms  offering allows products to provision and manage Supabase backends for their own users. Supabase cites AI builders such as Lovable and Bolt as examples of platforms using this model.
That is strategically interesting because it positions Supabase as  backend infrastructure underneath other developer/AI platforms , rather than merely competing for individual application developers.
Where I'd be cautious
Supabase isn't magic. The main things I'd pay attention to are:
• Postgres knowledge matters.  RLS in particular is extremely powerful, but getting authorization policies wrong can create security problems.
• You still need to understand backend architecture.  Supabase removes a lot of infrastructure work; it doesn't eliminate the need to design your data model and security correctly.
• Serverless/Edge constraints matter.  Edge Functions are excellent for short-lived API/webhook/AI orchestration tasks, but aren't necessarily the right place for heavy long-running computation.
• At large scale, architecture still matters.  "Postgres + Supabase" doesn't automatically solve high-volume  workloads, connection management, caching, queues, indexing, etc.
• You're still relying on a managed service  if you use Supabase Cloud, even though the underlying technology is open source.
My overall take
I'd describe Supabase as:
"PostgreSQL turned into a complete application backend."
And that's why it's become so popular. You get the power and maturity of Postgres while avoiding much of the traditional work involved in exposing it safely to an application.
It's particularly compelling for  SaaS, startups, internal tools, mobile/web apps, prototypes that may become production systems, and AI applications .
And yes , the  @supabase  account you mentioned is the official Supabase  presence on X; Supabase's own site links to its Twitter/X account.
If you're evaluating Supabase for a  specific project , I can also break down whether I'd choose  Supabase vs Firebase vs Neon vs AWS vs a custom Postgres backend , including cost, scalability, security and architecture.

prompt: What do you know about Supabase?
answer:
is an open-source-oriented
backend-as-a-service (BaaS)
platform. The simplest way to think about it is:
Supabase gives you a production-ready backend centered around PostgreSQL, without requiring you to build the backend infrastructure yourself.
What it provides
• PostgreSQL database  — a full Postgres database, rather than a proprietary database abstraction.
• Authentication  — email/password, magic links, OAuth providers, phone authentication, and more.
• Auto-generated APIs  — REST APIs and database access based on your Postgres schema.
• Realtime  — subscribe to database changes and build live features such as chat, collaborative apps, or dashboards.
• Storage  — object/file storage for images, videos, documents, etc., with access policies.
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript functions for custom backend logic.
• Row Level Security (RLS)  — PostgreSQL's security policies can control exactly which rows users are allowed to read or modify.
• Local development / self-hosting  — much of the platform is open source, and you can run Supabase locally or self-host it.
Why developers like it
The big selling point is the
Postgres-first architecture
. With something like Firebase, you generally adapt your application to Firebase's database and APIs. With Supabase, you get an actual PostgreSQL database, so you can use things like:
SQL
That makes Supabase particularly attractive when your application has
relational data
. For example, a SaaS app might have:
users
You can model those relationships naturally in Postgres and then expose the data through Supabase APIs.
A typical architecture
A modern application might look like:
┌─────────────────────┐
You can therefore build a surprisingly substantial application without running your own API server.
Where it shines
I'd seriously consider Supabase for:
• SaaS applications
• MVPs and startups
• Internal tools
• Dashboards
• Mobile apps
• CRUD-heavy applications
• Applications where relational data matters
• Apps that need authentication + database + file storage
• Real-time applications
The important caveat
Supabase isn't magic—you still need to understand
database design and security
, particularly PostgreSQL's
Row Level Security
. A poorly configured RLS policy can turn a seemingly secure application into one where users can access other users' data. Conversely, properly designed RLS can let you safely expose much of your database directly to clients without maintaining a traditional API layer. So I tend to think of Supabase less as "Firebase but open source" and more as:
Postgres + Auth + APIs + Realtime + Storage + serverless functions, packaged into a developer-friendly platform.
If you're considering using it for a particular project, tell me what you're building and I can explain
whether Supabase is a good fit, how I'd architect it, and what I'd watch out for.

• Storage  —  Object/file storage for things like images, videos, PDFs and other assets.
• Realtime  — Applications can subscribe to database changes and build things such  as collaborative interfaces, live dashboards and multiplayer experiences.
• Edge Functions  — Server-side TypeScript/Deno functions for webhooks, payments, APIs,  AI calls, email, scheduled-ish workloads, etc.
• Vector/AI capabilities  — PostgreSQL extensions such as  pgvector  can be used for storing and searching embeddings.
• Connection pooling  — Supabase provides Supavisor to handle database connections, particularly useful for serverless/edge workloads.

prompt: What do you know about Supabase (https://supabase.com/)?
answer:
is essentially a
developer-focused backend platform built around PostgreSQL
. The easiest mental model is:
“Firebase, but centered on a real Postgres database and with much more direct access to SQL.”
It has grown into a fairly comprehensive backend platform.
What Supabase gives you
A Supabase project includes several integrated services:
• PostgreSQL database  — a full Postgres database, not a proprietary database abstraction. You can use normal SQL, relationships, indexes, extensions, functions, triggers, etc.
• Authentication  — email/password, passwordless authentication, OAuth providers, and other login mechanisms.
• Row Level Security (RLS)  — PostgreSQL policies that can determine exactly which rows a particular user is allowed to access.
• Auto-generated APIs  — REST and GraphQL APIs over your database.
• Storage  — object/file storage for images, videos, PDFs, etc., with access policies integrated with your database.
• Realtime  — subscribe to database changes and synchronize state between clients.
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript/Deno functions for custom backend logic, webhooks, integrations, AI calls, etc.
• Vector/AI capabilities  — PostgreSQL extensions such as  pgvector  let you store and search embeddings.
• Cron and queues  — useful for scheduled/background processing.
• CLI and local development  — you can run much of the Supabase stack locally and manage database migrations/deployment.
• Self-hosting  — Supabase is open source and can be self-hosted.
So instead of assembling:
PostgreSQL
you can start with:
┌── Authentication
That's the core appeal.
The really important part: it's Postgres
This is probably the biggest distinction from something like Firebase. Supabase isn't hiding the relational database from you. Each project gets a
full PostgreSQL database
. You can work directly with tables, SQL, indexes, relationships, views, functions, triggers and Postgres extensions.
For example, you might have:
users
and use normal SQL:
SELECT *
That's a very powerful model for SaaS applications.
RLS is a big deal
One of Supabase's most important concepts is
Row Level Security
. You can expose your database to your frontend while having PostgreSQL enforce something like:
A user may read tasks belonging to projects belonging to organizations they're a member of.
The frontend doesn't have to rely solely on a backend endpoint like:
GET /api/my-tasks
Instead, the database itself can enforce the authorization policy. Supabase explicitly recommends protecting tables exposed through its Data API with RLS.
This is incredibly convenient—but it also means
understanding Postgres/RLS security becomes important
. Poorly designed policies can result in data exposure.
Edge Functions
When database queries and RLS aren't enough, you can write backend code using
Supabase Edge Functions
. They're TypeScript functions running on Supabase's edge infrastructure, using a Deno-compatible runtime. Typical uses include:
• Stripe webhooks
• calling external APIs
• sending emails
• AI/LLM orchestration
• privileged database operations
• custom APIs
• payment processing
• image processing
For example:
Browser
Supabase provides authentication mechanisms for these functions as well, including validating the user's JWT.
Where Supabase fits compared with other technologies
I'd roughly categorize the landscape like this:
Platform
Core philosophy
Supabase
PostgreSQL + integrated backend
Firebase
Google's managed backend + NoSQL-centric data model
Neon
Managed/serverless PostgreSQL
AWS
Assemble individual cloud services
Vercel
Frontend deployment + serverless/edge infrastructure
Clerk
Authentication/identity
PlanetScale
Managed database infrastructure
Appwrite
Open-source backend platform

prompt: What do you know about Supabase (@supabase on X/Twitter)?
answer:
is one of the most prominent open-source developer platforms, often described as an alternative to Firebase—but with  Postgres at the center rather than a proprietary NoSQL database .
What Supabase actually is
At its core, Supabase gives you a hosted  PostgreSQL database  plus a collection of backend services that sit around it:
• Postgres  — a full, ordinary PostgreSQL database that you can access directly with SQL.
• Authentication  — email/password, OAuth and other authentication flows, integrated with Postgres Row Level Security.
• Data APIs  — automatically generated REST APIs for your database.
• Realtime  — subscribe to database changes and build collaborative/live applications.
• Storage  — files such as images, videos and documents.
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript functions running without you managing servers.
• Vector/AI capabilities  — support for storing and searching embeddings, largely through Postgres/pgvector.
The important architectural distinction is that  Supabase doesn't try to hide Postgres from you . Its own documentation explicitly says that every project is a full Postgres database rather than an abstraction over one.
Why developers are excited about it
The killer proposition is essentially:
"Give me a production-grade backend without making me build the backend."
For example, you can create:
React/Next.js app → Supabase Auth → Postgres → RLS → Storage/Realtime/Edge Functions
without standing up your own API server, authentication system, database infrastructure, WebSocket infrastructure, etc.
And because the underlying database is Postgres, you're not learning a weird proprietary database API. You can use SQL, foreign keys, indexes, transactions, extensions, views, functions and PostgreSQL's broader ecosystem.
That's a big reason Supabase has become particularly popular with  indie hackers, startups, AI/vibe-coding developers and small engineering teams .
The open-source angle is important
Supabase is unusually committed to open source for a hosted developer platform. Its dashboard and many of its components are open source, and the company explicitly emphasizes self-hosting and portability.
In April 2026, Supabase announced that its GitHub repository had passed  100,000 stars  and said that  eight million developers  were building with Supabase.
Its current careers page says the company has  350+ employees, $1B raised and 540,000+ community members .
So this isn't really a tiny "Firebase clone" anymore. It's become a significant developer infrastructure company.
What about @supabase on X?
The Supabase brand has become particularly strong on developer social media. Their public presence tends to mix:
• product launches and technical announcements
• open-source projects
• Postgres content
• developer tutorials
• memes/community content
• AI-related tooling
• customer stories
• developer advocacy
That combination is quite deliberate. Supabase describes itself as a  "community of communities" , working across GitHub, Discord, Reddit, Twitter/X and Stack Overflow rather than treating the company account as merely a corporate marketing channel.
Where I think Supabase is strategically interesting
The really interesting part isn't simply  "Firebase but with Postgres."
It's the intersection of  Postgres + serverless + open source + AI .
AI-generated applications need somewhere to put:
• users
• application state
• relational data
• permissions
• files
• embeddings
• conversation history
• agent state
• search indexes
Postgres can handle a surprisingly large portion of that. Supabase is positioning itself as the infrastructure layer that makes all of this accessible to a developer who doesn't want to assemble 12 separate services.
And they're explicitly pushing toward this. Their current platform combines Postgres, Auth, Storage, Realtime, Edge Functions, APIs and vector embeddings in one platform.
One thing to watch out for
Supabase's simplicity can make it  look easier than it actually is .
The dangerous part isn't usually getting a prototype running. That's exceptionally easy.
The difficult parts are things like:
• designing good Postgres schemas
• correctly configuring  Row Level Security
• managing migrations
• connection pooling
• authorization architecture
• database performance
• Edge Function architecture
• avoiding accidentally exposing data through APIs
• understanding Postgres deeply enough when the application becomes large
Supabase itself puts considerable emphasis on RLS because your database is directly exposed through its APIs.
So I'd characterize it as:
Supabase is excellent at eliminating backend plumbing, but it doesn't eliminate backend engineering.
If you're interested because you've been seeing  @supabase  everywhere on X, I can also break down  why Supabase has become such a huge phenomenon on X, who is actually using it, how its business model works, who its real competitors are, and whether the company is likely to become a major infrastructure company.

answer:
Yes.
is one of the more important developer-infrastructure companies in the modern web stack, and its presence on X is unusually influential among developers.
What Supabase actually is
The simplest description is:
Supabase is a developer platform built around PostgreSQL.
Rather than being merely a database-as-a-service, it packages a Postgres database with many of the things an application needs around it:
• PostgreSQL  — every project gets a full Postgres database rather than a proprietary database abstraction.
• Authentication  — email/password, magic links, OTP, social login, SSO, etc.
• Row Level Security (RLS)  — database-level authorization policies.
• Auto-generated APIs  — REST APIs over your database.
• Storage  — files, images, videos, etc., with database/RLS integration.
• Realtime  — subscribe to database changes and synchronize state between clients.
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript/Deno functions.
• Vector/AI capabilities  — PostgreSQL-based vector storage/search and integrations.
• Cron, queues, GraphQL and other Postgres extensions/tools.
That's why their positioning is increasingly  "the Postgres development platform"  rather than simply "Firebase alternative."
The important architectural idea
Supabase's killer feature isn't any individual component. It's the integration between them.
For example:
Your application
Postgres is essentially the center of gravity. Auth, Storage, Realtime and other services are designed to work with the database and its authorization model.
That is a meaningful distinction from platforms where the database is largely hidden behind a proprietary API.
Why developers like it
A big reason is  developer experience .
You can go from:
"I have an idea"
to:
"I have a database, user accounts, APIs, file storage and realtime functionality"
very quickly.
And because the underlying database is PostgreSQL, you retain the ability to use SQL, Postgres extensions, normal database tooling, migrations, external Postgres clients, etc. Supabase explicitly describes its database as a  full Postgres database, not a Postgres abstraction .
That makes it particularly attractive for:
• SaaS applications
• startups
• prototypes/MVPs
• internal tools
• mobile apps
• AI applications
• developer tools
• marketplaces
• collaborative/realtime applications
Supabase also explicitly positions itself as infrastructure for  AI builders and frameworks , which is an increasingly important part of its strategy.
Supabase vs. Firebase
This is probably the most useful mental model.
Firebase  historically represented:
Google-managed backend primitives + NoSQL-centric architecture.
Supabase  represents:
Open-source-friendly backend primitives + PostgreSQL-centric architecture.
So if you're comfortable with SQL/Postgres, Supabase can feel much more natural than Firebase.
The tradeoff is that Supabase isn't magically "Postgres without complexity." Once your application becomes sophisticated, you still need to understand things like:
• indexes
• transactions
• query performance
• migrations
• RLS
• connection pooling
• database design
• backups/recovery
• permissions
That's actually part of its appeal:  it gives you a lot of real database power rather than hiding everything.
What makes their Edge Functions interesting
Supabase's Edge Functions are server-side TypeScript functions running on a Deno-compatible runtime. They're intended for things such as webhooks, integrations, lightweight backend logic and AI/LLM orchestration.

• database hosting
• auth provider
• API layer
• object storage
• realtime infrastructure
• serverless functions
That consolidation is the core Supabase proposition.
And @supabase on X?
The official account is  @supabase . The profile currently describes Supabase as "The Postgres development platform"; the X profile I found shows roughly  202K followers  and links to Supabase's site, GitHub, YouTube and Discord.
Their X presence is worth paying attention to because Supabase has built a fairly strong  developer-community/content distribution engine  around the product.
The account tends to revolve around things like:
• new product releases
• Postgres tips
• developer tutorials
• AI/app-building workflows
• demos
• integrations
• open-source projects
• community projects
• ecosystem announcements
So @supabase isn't just corporate PR. It's part of how the company drives adoption among developers.
The bigger strategic picture
This is the part I find most interesting.
Supabase is effectively  betting that  PostgreSQL becomes the foundational application database for the AI/software-building era , while Supabase becomes the easiest way to operate  that database plus the surrounding infrastructure.
The pitch is increasingly:
Don't build a backend infrastructure stack from scratch. Start with Postgres and let Supabase provide the platform around it.
And they're expanding beyond the traditional "backend for a React app" use case. Their documentation now explicitly describes Supabase as something other companies can themselves build platforms on top of, exposing database, Auth, Storage, Re altime and Edge Functions to their own users through APIs/MCP.
That makes Supabase potentially much more interesting than simply "Firebase but with Postgres."
In one sentence
Supabase is trying to make PostgreSQL feel like a complete, modern application platform rather than something you have to assemble and operate yourself.

prompt: What do you know about Supabase?
answer:
is an open-source backend-as-a-service platform built around
PostgreSQL
. It’s often described as an open-source alternative to Firebase, but its architecture is more directly centered on Postgres. Its main pieces are:
• Postgres database  — full PostgreSQL, including SQL, extensions, indexes, functions, triggers, and row-level security.
• Authentication  — email/password, magic links, OTP, social providers, and other auth flows.
• Auto-generated APIs  — REST APIs generated from your database schema, plus GraphQL options through its ecosystem.
• Realtime  — subscribe to database changes and build realtime features such as collaborative apps, notifications, dashboards, and chat.
• Storage  — object/file storage with access policies integrated with authentication.
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript functions running close to users, useful for webhooks, API endpoints, integrations, and backend logic.
• Dashboard & tooling  — database editor, SQL editor, logs, authentication management, storage management, migrations, and local development tooling.
• Local/self-hosted development  — Supabase provides tooling for running much of the stack locally, and the platform itself is open source.
Why developers like it
The biggest selling point is that
you aren't learning a proprietary database abstraction
. You get a real Postgres database underneath. For example, you can create:
create table projects (
Then combine that database with Supabase Auth and Row Level Security to control which users can access which rows. That makes Supabase particularly attractive for:
• SaaS applications
• Startups and MVPs
• AI applications that need persistent data
• Mobile/web apps
• Internal tools
• Multi-tenant applications
• Realtime applications
• Apps where you want SQL rather than a NoSQL database
Supabase vs. Firebase
The simplest mental model is:
Firebase:
Google ecosystem + proprietary databases/services + highly managed developer experience.
Supabase:
PostgreSQL + open-source ecosystem + managed developer experience. If you're comfortable with SQL/Postgres, Supabase can feel considerably more natural than Firebase.
One important caveat
Supabase isn't magic—you're still operating an actual PostgreSQL database. As an application grows, things like
schema design, indexes, query performance, migrations, RLS policies, connection management, backups, and database scaling
become important. For a serious application, I'd treat Supabase primarily as
managed Postgres with a very good set of surrounding backend services
, rather than simply "a Firebase clone." If you're considering Supabase for a particular project, I can also break down
its architecture, pricing, security/RLS model, Supabase vs. Firebase, or how I'd structure a production Supabase backend
.

prompt: What do you know about https://supabase.com/?
answer:
Yes.
is essentially a  backend-as-a-service built around PostgreSQL . Its pitch is: instead  of assembling a database, authentication system, file storage, APIs, realtime infrastructure, and serverless backend separately, you get them as one integrated platform.
What Supabase gives you
• PostgreSQL database  — Every project gets a full Postgres database, rather than a proprietary database abstraction. You can use SQL directly, create relationships, indexes, functions, triggers, etc.
• Authentication  — Email/password, passwordless, OAuth/social login, and other identity integrations. Auth is tightly integrated with Postgres and Row Level Security (RLS).
• Auto-generated APIs  — Your database can be accessed through ready-made REST APIs, so you don't necessarily  need to write CRUD endpoints yourself.
• Row Level Security  — One of Supabase's most important features. You can define rules such as  "users can only read their own records"  directly  in Postgres.
• Storage  — Upload and serve images, videos, documents, etc., with access controlled through policies.
• Realtime  — Subscribe to database changes and synchronize state between clients, useful for chat, collaboration, dashboards, multiplayer features, etc.
• Edge Functions  —  Server-side TypeScript/JavaScript functions running on Supabase's infrastructure, useful for webhooks, APIs, payment integrations, AI calls, and logic you don't want exposed to the browser .
• Vector/AI capabilities  — PostgreSQL can be used to store, index, and search vector embeddings, alongside other AI-oriented functionality.
• Cron and queues  — Supabase has also expanded beyond the traditional "Firebase alternative" model with scheduled jobs and queues.
A useful mental model
Imagine you're building a SaaS application:
Your App
The really interesting part is that  Postgres sits at the center . Auth, Storage, Realtime, APIs, and Functions are designed to work with that database rather than being disconnected services.
Why developers like it
The biggest advantage is  how much backend infrastructure you don't have to build yourself .
For example, a conventional application might require:
PostgreSQL + backend API + authentication provider + object storage + websocket infrastructure + background jobs + deployment infrastructure
With Supabase, a lot of that can become:
Supabase + your frontend
And you can still write normal SQL and backend code when you need more control.
It's also  open source and self-hostable , which is an important distinction from some purely proprietary BaaS products. Supabase explicitly emphasizes that you can inspect, contribute to, and self-host the software.
Supabase vs Firebase
A rough comparison:

If your application has things like  users → organizations → projects → memberships → subscriptions → invoices → permissions , I particularly like the Postgres/RLS approach because relational data and authorization rules fit together naturally.
One thing I'd pay particular attention to
Supabase makes it  very  easy to expose database functionality directly to your frontend. That's powerful, but it means  RLS isn't optional security decoration—it is fundamental to your architecture .
For example, you might have:
create policy "Users can see their own orders"
Then your frontend can query  orders , while Postgres itself enforces which rows the user is allowed to see.
That's a very different philosophy from:
Browser → Your API → authorization code → database
where all authorization lives in your application server.
Supabase can instead make it:
Browser → Supabase → Postgres/RLS
Edge Functions can still be used when you need privileged/server-side operations. Supabase's current documentation specifically supports scoping a function's database client to the caller's RLS policies while also providing a separate privileged client for operations that intentionally bypass RLS.
Where I think Supabase is especially compelling
I'd seriously consider it for:
• SaaS applications
• Internal business tools
• Mobile apps
• MVPs/startups
• AI applications and AI agents
• Dashboards
• Collaborative/realtime applications
• Applications where relational data matters
• Products being built rapidly with AI coding tools
It's particularly interesting for  AI-generated applications  right now: Supabase itself positions the platform toward AI builders, and its platform can be managed programmatically as well.
If  you're considering Supabase for a  specific project , tell me what you're building and I can go one level deeper—e.g.  whether I'd choose Supabase vs Firebase vs Neon + Auth0 vs a traditional backend, how I'd architect it, and what the likely costs/scaling issues would be.

prompt: What do you know about Supabase (https://supabase.com/)?
What do you know about Supabase (https://supabase.com/)?
answer:
is essentially a  backend-as-a-service built around PostgreSQL . Its pitch is: instead of assembling and maintaining a database, authentication system, file storage, APIs, realtime infrastructure, and serverless functions separately, you get them as one integrated platform.
What you get
• PostgreSQL database  — Every project gets  a real, full  Postgres database rather  than a proprietary  database abstraction. You  can use SQL , relationships, extensions , indexes, functions, etc .
• Authentication  — Email/password, magic  links, phone authentication , and social providers  such as Google , GitHub, Microsoft/A zure, Discord, etc . Authorization can be  enforced using Postgres  Row Level Security  (RLS).
• Auto-generated APIs  — Supabase can expose  your  database through  ready-to-use  APIs, so your  frontend can interact  with data without  you writing a  conventional CRUD backend  for everything.
• Storage  — Object/file storage  for images,  videos, documents, etc ., integrated with Postgres  and RLS-based  authorization.
• Realtime  — Clients can subscribe  to database changes , use presence , and  broadcast messages over  WebSockets.
• Edge Functions  — Server-side TypeScript  functions running on  Supabase's globally distributed  Edge Runtim e . They're useful for  webhooks, payments, API  endpoints, email, AI  calls, and other  backend logic.
• Vector/AI capabilities  — You  can store  and search vector  embeddings in Postgres , making Supabase useful  for RAG and  AI applications.
• Cron, queues, REST /GraphQL APIs and  other database extensions  are also part  of the current  platform.
Why developers like  it
The particularly nice architectural choice is that  Postgres is the center of the system .
For example, imagine you're building a SaaS application:
Your React / Next.js app
A user signs up → Supabase Auth manages the identity → their data lives in Postgres →  RLS  determines what they're allowed to see/change → Storage handles their files → Realtime can push changes to other clients → Edge Functions handle privileged/business logic.
That integration is one of Supabase's biggest strengths.
The really important part: Row Level Security
If you're evaluating Supabase seriously, I'd pay particular attention to  Postgres RLS .
Instead of relying exclusively on application code such as:
if user.id == record.owner_id:
you can make the database itself enforce the rule:
Users can only SELECT rows where
That means the authorization boundary lives close to the data. Supabase explicitly builds Auth and Storage authorization around Postgres/RLS.
It's extremely powerful, but it also means  you need to understand RLS properly . A badly designed policy can create security holes or make legitimate queries unexpectedly fail.
Supabase vs. Firebase
The comparison people most commonly make is:
Supabase ≈ Firebase, but with PostgreSQL at the center.

Supabase itself now explicitly positions its platform as open source and says you can self-host it, which is another meaningful distinction.
Where I think Supabase is particularly strong
I'd seriously consider it for:
• SaaS applications
• Internal tools
• Marketplaces
• Mobile apps
• CRUD-heavy applications
• Multi-tenant applications
• Dashboards
• Collaborative/realtime applications
• AI/RAG applications
• MVPs that may  eventually become substantial  production systems
• Applications where you  want  SQL rather than  a document database
It's especially attractive  for a small  team because you  can get quite  far without building  a traditional backend  infrastructure team.
Where I'd be more cautious
Supabase isn't magic. As an application becomes complex, you're still dealing with:
• PostgreSQL schema design
• indexes and query  performance
• migrations
• RLS policy complexity
• connection pooling
• background jobs
• observability
• rate limiting
• caching
• infrastructure/vendor considerations
• application-level business  logic
And Edge Functions  aren't intended to  replace arbitrary long -running backend workers ; Supabase's documentation  specifically notes that  cold starts can  occur and recommends  background workers for  heavy, long-running  jobs.
The other important  point is that "Supabase is open  source" doesn't mean  your hosted Supabase  project is equivalent  to simply running  PostgreSQL yourself . The managed service  gives you substantial  operational convenience , while self -hosting introduces infrastructure  responsibilities.
My overall take
If you're starting  a modern web  application today,  Supabase is one  of the first  backend platforms I'd  evaluate , particularly if you're  comfortable with SQL .
Its killer  feature isn't any  individual component. It's  the combination:
Postgres + Auth + RLS  + APIs + Storage + Realtime  + Functions
with a relatively  pleasant developer experience .
And because the  underlying database is  actually  PostgreSQL, you're not  starting with a  toy database that  you'll necessarily have  to migrate away  from once the  application becomes serious . Supabase's own documentation  describes each project  as a full  Postgres database and  supports backups and  point-in-time  recovery on paid  plans.
If you're  considering Supabase for a specific project , tell me what  you're building and  I can go  one level deeper —e.g.  architecture, security/RLS , pricing, Supabase vs  Firebase/Neon/PlanetScale , scaling limits, or  whether I'd actually  choose it for  your use case .

prompt: What do you know about Supabase (@supabase on X/Twitter)?
answer:
Yes.
is one of the more prominent developer infrastructure companies, and  @supabase  is its official presence on X.
What Supabase is
The simplest description is:
Supabase is a developer platform built around PostgreSQL that gives you most of the backend pieces needed to build an application.
Its core is a  real PostgreSQL database —not a proprietary database abstraction. Around that, Supabase provides:
• Postgres database  — SQL, relationships, indexes, extensions, etc.
• Authentication  — email/password, social login, OAuth, MFA, etc.
• Storage  — files, images, videos and other objects.
• Realtime  — subscribe to database changes and build realtime experiences.
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript/Deno functions.
• Auto-generated APIs  — APIs for interacting with your database.
• Vector/AI capabilities  — PostgreSQL-based vector storage and search.
• Row Level Security (RLS)  — database-level authorization policies.
The interesting philosophical difference from many "backend-as-a-service" products is that  Postgres remains yours and is directly accessible . You're not learning a completely proprietary data model that you later have to escape.
Why developers like it
Supabase became particularly popular because it dramatically reduces the amount of backend infrastructure you need to build yourself.
For example, instead of:
React/Next.js
you can have:
Supabase
That makes it particularly attractive for  startups, indie hackers, SaaS products, internal tools, mobile apps and AI applications  where getting a working product online quickly matters more than building every infrastructure component yourself.
The big strategic advantage: Postgres
This is probably the most important thing to understand about Supabase.
Supabase isn't really "Firebase but open source." Its stronger positioning is closer to:
"Postgres + a polished developer platform."
Every Supabase project gets a full Postgres database, and the surrounding services integrate with it.
That gives developers access to the enormous PostgreSQL ecosystem rather than locking them into a simplified NoSQL-style data model.
For example, you can use:
SELECT *
and then build authentication, authorization, APIs, realtime behavior and application logic around that database.
How Supabase makes money
The business model is primarily cloud infrastructure/software subscriptions plus usage.
As of September 2026, the advertised plans include  Free, Pro, Team and Enterprise . Pro starts at  $25/month , with additional usage-based charges depending on resources.
The free tier is surprisingly generous: it currently includes 500 MB of database storage, 1 GB of file storage, 50,000 MAU, 2 million Realtime messages and 500,000 Edge Function invocations. Free projects can, however, be paused after inactivity.

prompt: What do you know about https://supabase.com/ and @supabase on X/Twitter?
answer:
Yes.
is one of the more important developer-platform companies in the modern web/AI stack. I checked both its current site and recent activity around its official X account.
What Supabase actually is
Supabase describes itself as
“the Postgres development platform.”
The simplest mental model is:
Supabase = managed Postgres + authentication + APIs + storage + realtime + server-side functions, packaged into a developer-friendly platform.
The important distinction is that
Postgres is the foundation
, rather than an implementation detail hidden behind a proprietary database abstraction. Each project gets a real Postgres database that you can connect to directly.
Its main pieces include:
• Postgres  — the core relational database.
• Auth  — email/password, OAuth and other authentication mechanisms, with Row Level Security (RLS).
• Data APIs  — automatically exposed APIs for working with database data.
• Realtime  — subscribe to database changes and synchronize data in real time.
• Storage  — files such as images, videos and documents.
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript functions.
• Vector  — storing and querying embeddings for AI/RAG applications.
• Dashboard/Studio  — visual database and infrastructure management.
There's also a significant
open-source/self-hosting philosophy
. Supabase says explicitly that its stack is open source and designed to avoid vendor lock-in; you can inspect, contribute to and self-host the software.
Why developers like it
The killer proposition is
how much backend infrastructure you get without building it yourself
. For example, a small SaaS application might need:
Frontend
Instead of assembling a database provider, auth provider, object-storage provider, API layer and realtime infrastructure separately, you can get them as one integrated system. And because it's Postgres, you're not learning some proprietary database language or giving up the relational model. Supabase emphasizes that you have access to the underlying Postgres database rather than being trapped behind an abstraction.
That's particularly attractive for:
• SaaS products
• mobile apps
• prototypes that need to become production applications
• AI applications
• internal tools
• marketplaces
• applications generated with AI coding tools
The last category has become particularly interesting: Supabase is increasingly positioning itself as
infrastructure for AI-generated applications
, not merely as a Firebase alternative.
Supabase and AI
This is probably one of the most interesting things about the company right now. Supabase has been expanding beyond the traditional "database + auth" story toward being a backend layer for
AI agents and AI-generated software
. Its recent product updates include things such as:
• vector/embedding support
• MCP-related integrations
• integrations with AI coding agents
• an official Supabase ChatGPT app
• integrations with tools such as OpenCode
• database branching/developer workflows
• improved support for AI-oriented development.
That's strategically important because an AI coding agent can generate a frontend fairly easily, but the resulting application still needs
persistent state, users, permissions, files, database queries and server-side logic
. Supabase is increasingly trying to be the layer that supplies that backend.
What about
@supabase
on X?
The official account is
@supabase
, and it's an unusually important part of the company's developer/community strategy. Supabase uses X heavily for:
• product announcements
• developer updates
• launch announcements
• ecosystem integrations
• community interaction
• technical discussions
• responding to incidents
• showcasing things developers build
A good example of the latter is the way Supabase communicated during the
2026 India access disruption
. In February 2026, Supabase publicly acknowledged that some Indian ISPs were blocking access and said its infrastructure itself remained operational.
So I wouldn't view
@supabase
merely as a corporate marketing account.
Their social presence is deeply integrated into their developer-relations strategy.
The bigger competitive picture
The interesting comparison isn't simply:
Supabase vs. PostgreSQL
It's more like:
Supabase vs. Firebase vs. AWS/GCP/Azure building blocks vs. specialized backend services.
Supabase's thesis is essentially:
Start with the power and maturity of Postgres, then make the surrounding backend infrastructure ridiculously easy to use.
That's different from Firebase's original philosophy, which centered around Google's own backend primitives and historically emphasized NoSQL. Supabase itself explicitly says it isn't simply making a 1:1 Firebase clone; its architecture is deliberately centered around Postgres and open-source components.
One thing I'd watch carefully
Supabase's greatest strength—
making powerful infrastructure incredibly easy to spin up—is also where some of the engineering risk lies.
It's easy to create something that works:
create database
It's considerably harder to make the resulting application
secure and production-grade
. In particular, Supabase makes
Postgres Row Level Security
extremely important. If your authorization policies are poorly designed, having a convenient automatically exposed API doesn't magically make the application secure. Supabase has actually been tightening defaults in this area. For example, it announced that new tables in the public schema would no longer automatically be exposed through its Data API, with enforcement rolling out during 2026.
My overall take
I'd put Supabase in the category of
companies that are quietly becoming foundational infrastructure for the AI-native software ecosystem
. Its original pitch was roughly:
"The open-source Firebase alternative built around Postgres."
Its more interesting 2026 pitch is becoming:
"The backend that lets humans and AI agents build real applications extremely quickly."
That evolution is worth watching. And if you're asking because you're evaluating
Supabase as a company, its business model, its technology, its X strategy, or whether you should build/use something around its ecosystem
, I can go considerably deeper into that angle.

prompt: What do you know about Supabase (https://supabase.com/, @supabase on X/Twitter)?
answer:
What is Supabase?
is a  backend-as-a-service / Postgres development platform . The simplest mental model is:
“Firebase, but centered around PostgreSQL and open-source infrastructure.”
Its core idea is that instead of building a backend from scratch—database, authentication, APIs, file storage, realtime infrastructure, serverless functions—you start with a managed  PostgreSQL database  and get those services integrated around it.
The main pieces
• Postgres database  — Every project gets a full PostgreSQL database, rather than a proprietary  database abstraction. You can use normal SQL, foreign keys, extensions, indexes, functions, etc.
• Authentication  — Email/password, social login and other authentication flows , with authorization commonly handled through PostgreSQL  Row Level Security (RLS) .
• Auto-generated APIs  — Supabase can expose your database through REST APIs, with GraphQL also available.
• Storage  — Object/file storage for things such as images, videos and documents , with permissions integrated with Postgres.
• Realtime  — Clients can subscribe to database changes and receive updates over WebSockets.
• Edge Functions  — Server -side TypeScript/JavaScript functions for custom APIs, webhooks, background-ish workloads and integrations.
• Vector / AI capabilities  — PostgreSQL-based vector storage and search for embeddings, making it useful for RAG and AI applications.
• Dashboard / tooling  — Table editor, SQL editor, authentication management, database advisors, logs, etc.
The interesting architectural choice is that these aren't completely independent services glued together.  Postgres is the center of gravity.  Auth, Storage, Realtime and other components integrate closely with it.
Why developers like it
The biggest advantage is  speed without throwing away SQL .
For example, you can create:
React / Next.js app
A surprisingly large amount of backend infrastructure can therefore be replaced by a relatively small amount of application code.
It's particularly attractive for:
• SaaS applications
• startups and MVPs
• dashboards /admin applications
• mobile apps
• marketplaces
• collaborative/realtime applications
• AI applications with embeddings/RAG
• prototypes that you expect to eventually become serious  products
Supabase itself currently positions the platform around everything from weekend projects to applications scaling to millions of users.
The really important part: it's PostgreSQL
This is what distinguishes Supabase from many "backend as a service" products.
If you use Supabase, you're not learning some proprietary query language and hoping the platform eventually gives you an escape hatch.  You're working with PostgreSQL.
That means you can use:
CREATE TABLE customers (
and then use normal PostgreSQL capabilities—relationships, transactions, indexes, SQL queries, functions, extensions, etc.
Supabase explicitly describes each project as a  full Postgres database, not a Postgres abstraction .
That's a very strong proposition for developers who understand relational databases.
And it's genuinely open source
This is another major part of the company's identity.
The Supabase stack includes open-source components such as PostgREST, GoTrue, Realtime and Storage, and Supabase provides a self-hosting option. Its architecture is deliberately composed from open-source technologies rather than being a single opaque proprietary backend.
That's why you'll sometimes hear Supabase described as  "the open-source Firebase alternative."
I think that's directionally correct, although  "Postgres development platform"  is a better description of what it has become.
Supabase vs Firebase
A simplified comparison:

If your application has lots of relationships—users → organizations → projects → memberships → permissions → invoices, for example— Postgres can be a huge advantage .
One thing you should pay particular attention to: RLS
Supabase's  Row Level Security  is one of its most powerful features, but also one of the easiest things to get wrong.
Instead of putting all authorization logic in your application server, you can make the database enforce rules such as:
A user can read rows only where  user_id = auth.uid() .
That means even if your frontend makes a query directly against Supabase, the database itself determines which records that user is allowed to see.
This is one of the reasons Supabase can work without the traditional:
Frontend → Backend API → Database
architecture.
You can have:
Frontend → Supabase API → PostgreSQL
with the database enforcing authorization.
That's extremely powerful—but  bad RLS policies can create serious security vulnerabilities , so I'd consider understanding RLS essential before deploying a production Supabase application.
What Supabase isn't
It's not really a replacement for  everything  in a backend.
For complicated applications you may still want:
• a dedicated application server
• queues/workers
• specialized caching
• complex background processing
• Kubernetes/container infrastructure
• dedicated analytics infrastructure
• other databases or search systems
Supabase is best thought of as  a very capable backend foundation , rather than a magical replacement for every piece of infrastructure.
And @supabase on X
Supabase has built a notably strong developer/community presence around its
and open-source ecosystem. Their own site emphasizes community contributions, GitHub, Discord and developer resources alongside the commercial platform.
One interesting indicator of its current positioning is the emphasis on  AI applications and AI-assisted development : Supabase now explicitly markets vector/embedding functionality and has integrations/tool ing aimed at AI builders.
My one-sentence take
Supabase is essentially a managed PostgreSQL platform that gives developers most of the backend primitives needed to build a modern web/mobile/AI application—while keeping SQL, PostgreSQL and open-source infrastructure at the center.
If you're evaluating Supabase for a  specific project , I can also break down  whether I'd choose  Supabase vs Firebase vs Neon vs PlanetScale vs a traditional Postgres backend , including the architectural and  cost tradeoffs.

prompt: What do you know about Supabase?
answer:
is an open -source backend-as -a -service platform built  around  PostgreSQL . It’s often described  as an open -source alternative to  Firebase, but  its PostgreSQL foundation  gives it a  somewhat different architecture  and developer experience .
What Supabase provides
• Postgres database  — a full PostgreSQL  database, including SQL , extensions, indexes, functions , triggers,  and relational data  modeling.
• Authentication  — email/password, magic  links, OAuth providers , social login, MFA , and more.
• Auto-generated APIs  — REST APIs generated  from your database  schema, plus GraphQL  support  through its ecosystem .
• Realtime  — subscribe to database  changes and build  realtime features such  as collaborative  apps, notifications, or  live dashboards.
• Storage  — object/file storage  with access policies  integrated with  Supabase Auth.
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript  functions for APIs , webhooks, integrations , and backend logic .
• Row Level Security  (RLS)  — PostgreSQL's security  policies can  be used to  control exactly which  rows authenticated users  can access.
• Local development  — a CLI and  Docker-based  local stack let  you develop against  a local Supabase  environment.
Why developers like  it
The big architectural  advantage is that your database is  a real PostgreSQL  database , rather than a  proprietary database abstraction .
For example, you  can model:
users
and use ordinary  SQL, foreign keys , constraints, transactions , indexes, views , and PostgreSQL functions .
Then Supabase can  expose that database  to your frontend  while  RLS policies enforce  authorization at the  database level .
That makes it  particularly attractive  for applications where  the data model  is relational—S aaS applications, marketplaces , dashboards, internal tools , CRMs, collaboration apps , etc.
A typical stack
A modern application  might look something  like:
React / Next.js
You don't necessarily  need to build  a conventional backend  server for every  application. Supabase can  handle much of  the infrastructure while  you write application -specific logic  where necessary.
The part I'd  pay the most  attention to
If you're evaluating  Supabase,  RLS is probably  the most important  concept to understand .
It's extremely powerful , but it also  means you need  to think carefully  about authorization policies . A badly configured  policy can accidentally  expose data, while  a well-designed  policy can make  the database itself  enforce your application's  security model.
Supabase is also  particularly interesting  if you're building  with  AI/LLM applications , because PostgreSQL +  pgvector  can provide relational  data, embeddings/vector  search, authentication,  and  application storage in  one platform.
If you're considering  using Supabase for  a specific project , tell me what  you're building and  I can explain whether I'd choose  Supabase, Firebase, a  traditional backend, or  something like Neon  + a separate API  for it.

prompt: What do you know about https://supabase.com/?
answer:
Yes.
is essentially a  backend-as-a-service built around PostgreSQL . Its pitch is: instead of building and operating a backend from scratch, you get a production-ready Postgres database plus the common backend services your application needs.
What you get
• PostgreSQL database  — every project gets a real Postgres database, rather than a proprietary database abstraction. You can use SQL, extensions, foreign keys, views, triggers, etc.
• Authentication  — email/password, passwordless, OAuth/social login, and other authentication options.
• Row Level Security (RLS)  — PostgreSQL's security policies can control exactly which rows each user can access. This is one of Supabase's biggest strengths.
• Auto-generated APIs  — your database can be accessed through APIs without you having to manually build CRUD endpoints.
• Storage  — file storage for things like images, PDFs and videos, integrated with Postgres/RLS.
• Realtime  — clients can subscribe to database changes and other realtime events.
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript functions running on Supabase's edge infrastructure, useful for webhooks, custom APIs, payments, AI calls, etc.
• Vector/AI capabilities  — you can store and search vector embeddings alongside your Postgres data.
• Cron, queues, REST and GraphQL APIs  and other database-oriented features.
A useful way to think about it
Suppose you're building a SaaS application.
Without Supabase, you might have:
React / Next.js
With Supabase, you can have:
React / Next.js
That's why it's particularly attractive for  startups, SaaS applications, internal tools, mobile apps, AI applications and rapid prototypes .
The really important part: it's PostgreSQL
This is where I think Supabase differs significantly from the way people sometimes describe it as "Firebase but open source."
Firebase is fundamentally built around  Google's own database model. Supabase gives you  actual PostgreSQL .
That means you can use normal relational database concepts:
users
with relationships, indexes, constraints, transactions, SQL queries,  database functions, triggers, etc.
And you aren't limited to accessing it through Supabase's JavaScript SDK—you can connect to Post gres using standard database connection methods as well. Supabase provides different connection/pooling modes for traditional servers , serverless applications and edge functions.
Where I think Supabase is particularly good
1. Building a SaaS quickly
For example:
Next.js + Supabase + Stripe
can give you a surprisingly complete SaaS stack:
Supabase Auth       → users
2. AI applications
This is another area where Supabase has become interesting. You can keep application data,  users, permissions and vector embeddings in the same Postgres ecosystem rather than immediately introducing several databases.
3. Applications with complicated permissions
RLS is extremely powerful. Instead of trusting your frontend to say "this user can access this record," you can  make the database itself enforce the rule.
For example, conceptually:
User A → can see rows belonging to Organization A
The database enforces it.
4. Rapid development
You can create a database table, authentication system and APIs very quickly. Supabase also provides a dashboard with things like a Table Editor, SQL Editor and R LS policy management.
Is it actually "serverless"?
Sort of —but I wouldn't think of Supabase simply as a serverless database.
It's more accurate to think of it as:
Managed PostgreSQL + a collection of tightly integrated backend services.
And you can use as much or as little of it as you want. Supabase explicitly positions the individual products as integrated but independently useful.
One thing I would be careful about
Supabase makes it very easy to build something quickly, but  easy doesn't automatically mean correctly secured .
The biggest thing I'd learn before building anything serious is  Postgres Row Level Security . A poorly designed RLS policy can expose data; conversely, well-designed RLS can give you a very strong authorization layer.
Also, while Supabase  emphasizes that the platform is open source and self-hostable, using the hosted Supabase service still means you're relying on their managed infrastructure.
If you're asking because you're considering  using Supabase for a particular application , tell me what you're building. I can map out  exactly how I'd structure the Supabase database, Auth, RLS policies, APIs and Edge Functions  for it—and also tell you whether Supabase is the right choice versus Firebase, AWS, Neon, or a conventional Postgres backend.

prompt: What do you know about Supabase (https://supabase.com/)?
answer:
Yes.
is essentially a
backend-as-a-service built around PostgreSQL
. Its big appeal is that you can get a production-capable backend without assembling and operating every backend component yourself.
What Supabase gives you
At the center is a
real PostgreSQL database
—not a proprietary database abstraction. Each project gets its own Postgres database, with Supabase layering additional services around it.
• Postgres database  — tables, relationships, SQL, indexes, extensions, functions, triggers, etc.
• Authentication  — email/password, passwordless, OAuth, mobile authentication, and integration with third-party auth providers.
• Row Level Security (RLS)  — database-level policies controlling which users can read/write which rows.
• Auto-generated APIs  — access your Postgres data through REST and other APIs.
• Storage  — files such as images, videos, documents, with access controlled through policies.
• Realtime  — subscribe to database changes, broadcast messages, and track presence.
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript/Deno functions for APIs, webhooks, integrations, background-ish tasks, etc.
• Vector/AI capabilities  — vector embeddings and search, useful for RAG and AI applications.
• Cron and queues  — for scheduled and asynchronous workloads.
• Dashboard + CLI  — manage the database, SQL, policies, deployments, logs, etc.
• Self-hosting  — much of the platform is open source and can be run yourself. Supabase explicitly positions itself around avoiding vendor lock-in.
The architecture is particularly interesting
A typical Supabase application might look like:
Your Web / Mobile App
The important part is that
Postgres is the foundation
. Auth, Storage, Realtime, and other services integrate with it rather than feeling like completely separate products.
That makes Supabase particularly attractive if you're comfortable with SQL.
Why developers like it
The biggest advantage, in my view, is
how much backend infrastructure you get while retaining the mental model of Postgres
. For example, instead of building:
React/Next.js → API server → ORM → PostgreSQL → authentication server → object storage → WebSocket infrastructure
you can often do:
React/Next.js → Supabase → PostgreSQL
with Supabase handling a lot of the plumbing. And you aren't giving up SQL in exchange. You can still use normal Postgres features and connect to the database directly when appropriate.
RLS is a particularly powerful feature
You can put authorization rules directly at the database layer. For example, conceptually:
create policy "Users can see their own documents"
Now the database itself enforces that rule. Your frontend doesn't have to be trusted to remember to filter out somebody else's documents. Supabase recommends protecting exposed tables with RLS when using its Data APIs.
Supabase vs Firebase
The simplest mental model is:
Supabase ≈ Firebase, but Postgres-centric rather than Google/Firestore-centric.
