I would generally find Postgres/Supabase a very natural fit.
Where it gets especially interesting for AI
Supabase has increasingly positioned itself as infrastructure for
AI applications
, not merely a Firebase alternative. You can store embeddings in Postgres, perform vector search, combine vector similarity with normal relational queries, and use Edge Functions to orchestrate calls to external AI models. That means an AI application can potentially have:
LLM
That's one reason Supabase has become popular in the current AI-app ecosystem.
One thing I'd be careful about
Supabase makes it
very easy to build something quickly
, but that doesn't automatically make the architecture correct. The areas I'd pay particular attention to are:
• RLS policy design
• database indexes and query performance
• connection pooling
• secrets/API keys
• Edge Function architecture
• migrations
• backups/recovery
• separating trusted server operations from client-accessible operations
• avoiding excessive reliance on frontend-side authorization
For example, Supabase's current guidance distinguishes between client-facing Data API access, Edge Functions, and direct Postgres connections depending on the security and execution model you need.
My overall take
If you're building a
modern web app, SaaS, internal tool, marketplace, mobile app, or AI application
, Supabase is one of the platforms I'd seriously consider today. Its killer combination is:
Postgres + Auth + RLS + Storage + Realtime + APIs + serverless functions
without requiring you to operate all of that infrastructure yourself. And unlike many "backend-as-a-service" products,
you still fundamentally own a PostgreSQL architecture
, which makes it considerably less of a black box. If you're considering Supabase for a particular project, tell me what you're building and your stack (e.g.
Next.js, React, Flutter, Python, etc.
). I can then explain
exactly how I'd architect it with Supabase
, including database schema, auth/RLS, APIs, Edge Functions, and deployment.

prompt: What do you know about Supabase (@supabase on X/Twitter)?
answer:
Yes.  Supabase  is one of the more important developer-platform companies in the modern web/AI stack, and  @supabase  is its official presence on X.
What Supabase actually is
The simplest description is:
Supabase is a developer platform built around PostgreSQL that gives you most of the backend infrastructure needed to build an application.
A Supabase project gives you a full Postgres database plus:
• Authentication  — email/password, passwordless, OAuth, SSO, etc.
• Database APIs  — automatically generated REST/GraphQL APIs.
• Row Level Security (RLS)  — database-level authorization policies.
• Storage  — files such as images, videos and documents.
• Realtime  — subscribe to database changes and synchronize state between clients.
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript/JavaScript functions.
• Vector/AI capabilities  — particularly useful for embeddings and AI applications.
• Database tooling  — migrations, branching, backups, extensions, connection pooling, etc.
The important architectural decision is that  Postgres is the center of the system . Supabase isn't trying to hide the database behind a proprietary abstraction; each project has an actual Postgres database that you can connect to directly.
Why developers like it
Supabase became particularly popular because it makes a traditional backend feel almost instantaneous to set up.
For example, instead of building:
React/Next.js app → API server → authentication system → database → file storage → realtime infrastructure
you can have:
React/Next.js → Supabase
with Postgres, Auth, Storage, APIs and Realtime already integrated.
That makes it especially attractive for:
• startups
• indie hackers
• SaaS applications
• prototypes/MVPs
• internal tools
• mobile apps
• AI applications
• "vibe-coded" applications
Its own positioning is essentially  "Postgres development platform" , rather than merely "Firebase but open source." Supabase explicitly distinguishes itself from Firebase by putting PostgreSQL—not a NoSQL database—at the core.
The open-source angle is important
Supabase is unusually open for a hosted developer platform. Its architecture uses and contributes to open-source projects, and the Supabase platform itself can be self-hosted.
That gives developers an appealing property:
You aren't fundamentally building on a proprietary database.
Your underlying data is PostgreSQL, so you can  use SQL, Postgres extensions, standard database tooling, and eventually migrate elsewhere if necessary.
That doesn't mean migration is literally effortless—there are still Supabase-specific pieces such  as Auth, Storage, APIs and Realtime—but the database itself is highly portable.
Supabase and AI
This is where  @supabase  has become particularly interesting.
AI-generated applications need a surprisingly large amount of backend infrastructure: user  accounts, databases, embeddings, file uploads, permissions, APIs, background processing, etc.
Supabase provides many of those primitives in one place, including vector storage/search  through Postgres extensions and tooling aimed at AI builders.
That's one reason Supabase fits so naturally into the current "AI coding"  ecosystem: an AI coding agent can create a database schema, authentication, RLS policies and application code without a human having to assemble a dozen separate infrastructure  services.

Postgres + Firebase-like developer experience + open source + excellent APIs + increasingly strong AI/developer tooling.

prompt: What do you know about Supabase (https://supabase.com/, @supabase on X/Twitter)?
answer:
What is Supabase?
is an  open-source backend platform built around PostgreSQL . The easiest mental model is:
“Firebase, but centered on Postgres and with much more direct access to the underlying database.”
Its goal is to give developers most of the infrastructure needed to build a modern application without having to assemble and operate each backend component separately.
The core pieces
• Postgres database  — Every project gets a full PostgreSQL database rather than a proprietary database abstraction. You can use normal SQL, Postgres extensions, indexes, functions, triggers, etc.
• Authentication  — Email/password, magic links, OTP, social login, SSO and other authentication mechanisms.  Auth integrates closely with Postgres and Row Level Security (RLS).
• Auto-generated APIs  — Your database can be accessed through REST APIs  and other data APIs, with permissions governed by Postgres/RLS.
• Row Level Security  — One of Supabase's most important features. You can express rules such as “users may only read rows belonging to themselves”  directly in Postgres policies.
• Storage  — Object/file storage for things like images, videos  and documents, integrated with database access policies.
• Realtime  — WebSocket-based synchronization, including database changes, presence and broadcast messaging.
• Edge Functions  — Server-side TypeScript functions running on Supabase's edge infrastructure, useful for webhooks, APIs, integrations and small AI workloads.
• Vector/AI capabilities  — PostgreSQL-based vector storage and search, alongside tools for building AI applications.
• Cron, queues and additional Postgres tooling  — Increasingly, Supabase is positioning itself as a broader application backend rather than merely “hosted Postgres.”
Why developers like it
The particularly powerful part is that these aren't completely separate products glued together.
For example, imagine you're building a SaaS application:
React / Next.js / mobile app
A user's authentication identity can map naturally to database permissions, and those permissions can determine which records the user can access. That's a very attractive architecture for small teams because  the database becomes the center of the backend  rather than something hidden behind several layers of proprietary services.
Supabase vs. Firebase
The simplest comparison is:

Supabase explicitly emphasizes that its platform is built in the open and can be self-hosted, which is an important philosophical difference from Firebase.
Where it gets especially interesting
Supabase has become particularly popular for  AI-generated/vibe-coded applications . Its combination of a database, authentication, APIs, storage and functions means an AI coding tool can create a surprisingly complete application without someone manually designing an entire backend infrastructure.
Supabase itself highlights customers such as Lovable, Chatbase and eXp Realty, and currently positions the platform toward AI builders as well as conventional developers.
It's also increasingly useful for AI applications because Postgres can serve as the system of record while storing vector embeddings and application data alongside the rest of the application's relational data.
The important caveat
Supabase  doesn't eliminate backend engineering .
The biggest thing to understand is that exposing a Postgres-backed API directly to a frontend is safe only if your authorization model—particularly your  RLS policies—is designed correctly . Supabase's documentation explicitly recommends protecting exposed tables with RLS and carefully controlling privileges.
For a toy app, Supabase can feel almost magical.
For a production application, you still need to think carefully about:
• database schema design
• RLS and authorization
• migrations
• indexes/query performance
• connection pooling
• secrets
• API abuse/rate limiting
• backups and  recovery
• server-side business logic
• observability
• costs at scale
So I would describe Supabase as  “managed Postgres plus a very well-integrated application backend” , rather than simply “a backend-as-a-service.”
And as of 2026, that's probably the most important thing about it:  Supabase has evolved from “open-source Firebase alternative” into a fairly comprehensive Postgres-centered application platform.
If you're evaluating it for a specific  project, I can also break down  Supabase vs. Firebase vs. Neon vs. AWS , including architecture, pricing, scalability, lock-in, and when I'd choose each one.

prompt: What do you know about Supabase?
answer:
is an open-source backend platform that gives developers a lot of what they’d traditionally build themselves around a database. At its core, Supabase provides:
• Postgres database  — a full PostgreSQL database, rather than a proprietary database abstraction.
• Authentication  — email/password, magic links, social login, OAuth, and other auth mechanisms.
• Storage  — object/file storage for things like images, videos, and documents.
• Realtime  — subscribe to database changes and build realtime features.
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript functions for backend logic.
• Auto-generated APIs  — APIs are generated from your Postgres schema, making it quick to build applications.
• Row Level Security (RLS)  — PostgreSQL's security policies can control exactly which rows a user is allowed to read or modify.
• Dashboard and tooling  — a web interface for managing databases, users, storage, SQL, logs, etc.
Why developers like it
The big appeal is that
you get the convenience of a Backend-as-a-Service while retaining PostgreSQL
. For example, you could build an application with:
React / Next.js
You don't necessarily need to build a conventional backend API from scratch. A particularly powerful pattern is:
Postgres + RLS + Supabase Auth
You can put authorization rules directly alongside your database schema. For example, a policy can ensure that users only see rows where
user_id = auth.uid()
.
Where it fits
I'd generally think of Supabase as a strong choice for:
• SaaS applications
• MVPs and startups
• Internal tools
• Mobile/web apps
• Dashboards
• Multi-tenant applications
• Applications that need realtime functionality
• Projects where you want a conventional SQL/Postgres database rather than a NoSQL system
It's often compared with platforms such as Firebase, but the fundamental philosophy is different:
Supabase is built around PostgreSQL and open-source technologies
, whereas Firebase is centered around Google's proprietary backend ecosystem. If you're considering Supabase for a particular project, I can also explain
its architecture, pricing, security/RLS model, Supabase vs Firebase, or how I'd structure a production Supabase project
.

prompt: What do you know about https://supabase.com/?
answer:
Yes.
is essentially a  backend-as-a-service built around PostgreSQL . Its big selling point is that you get a real Postgres database plus the common backend pieces you would otherwise have to assemble yourself.
What Supabase gives you
• PostgreSQL database  — every project gets a full Postgres database, rather than a proprietary database abstraction. You can use SQL directly.
• Authentication  — email/password, passwordless, OAuth and other login mechanisms, integrated with  the database's security model.
• Row Level Security (RLS)  — one of Supabase's most important features. You can define database policies such as " users can only read their own records."
• Auto-generated APIs  — your database can be accessed through Supabase's APIs/client  libraries without you having to build a conventional CRUD API for everything.
• Storage  — file storage for things such as images, videos and documents, integrated with  Postgres/RLS.
• Realtime  — clients can subscribe to database changes and synchronize state in real time.
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript /Deno functions for things like webhooks, payments, AI calls and custom APIs.
• Vector/AI capabilities  — it supports storing, indexing and searching vector embeddings,  alongside other database extensions and AI-oriented tooling.
• Cron, queues and other Postgres extensions  — useful once your application  becomes more sophisticated.
The mental model
Think of a typical application:
Your Web / Mobile App
The interesting part is that  Postgres sits at the center . Auth, Storage, Realtime and the other services integrate around it.
Why developers like it
The biggest advantage is  speed without giving up SQL .
Instead of building:
PostgreSQL + authentication service + object storage + API server + realtime infrastructure + serverless functions
you can start with Supabase and get most of that as one integrated platform.
It's particularly attractive for:
• SaaS applications
• MVPs and startups
• dashboards/admin systems
• mobile apps
• marketplaces
• collaborative/realtime apps
• AI applications
• applications that need relational data
• applications being built with AI coding tools
Supabase itself now explicitly positions the platform toward AI builders, and its site highlights integrations with AI tooling and AI-generated applications.

Is Supabase "just a database"?
No—and that's an important distinction.
You  can  use it simply as hosted Postgres. But its real value is the integrated stack:
Postgres + Auth + RLS + APIs + Storage + Realtime + server-side functions.

’s official X account is  @supabase :
. It currently has roughly  202K followers  and describes itself as “The Postgres development platform.”
What the account is about
The account is essentially Supabase’s  developer-facing media and community channel . Its content tends to revolve around:
• Product launches and  features  — Postgres, Auth, Storage , Realtime, Edge Functions , Vector/AI capabilities , etc. Supabase  positions these as  an integrated developer  platform built around  Postgres.
• Postgres and open  source  — They frequently amplify  PostgreSQL, pgvector,  PostgREST, Deno and  other projects in  the ecosystem rather  than treating Supabase  as an isolated  proprietary stack.
• Launch-week marketing  — Supabase has historically  used “Launch Week ” as a major  mechanism for announcing  clusters of new  features.
• Developer education/content  — Tutorials, demos, technical  explanations, templates  and examples.
• Community engagement  — Reposts/replies to  developers building with  Supabase, community projects , contributors and ecosystem  partners.
• AI/vibe-coding  positioning  — More recently, Supabase  has been increasingly  associated with the  AI-app-building  ecosystem, particularly  as a backend /database layer for  AI-generated applications .
The interesting thing  about their X  strategy
Supabase is unusually  good at  making a developer  tool feel like  a developer movement .
Their broader philosophy  is explicitly open -source and community -driven. Supabase says  it has been  open source from  day one and  emphasizes supporting existing  open-source communities  rather than reinventing  everything itself.
That shows up  on X: rather  than every post  being  “here's our new  SaaS feature, buy  it,”  the account can  talk about  Postgres, open source , developers, benchmarks , interesting projects and  the people building  things .

My read on  the brand

technical + playful + developer -native + community-oriented  + product-aware
It's not trying  to sound like  a traditional enterprise  software company. The  brand generally assumes  that its audience  already understands developer  culture and is  comfortable with things  like Postgres, GitHub , open source, frameworks , memes and shipping  quickly.
And that's probably  one reason  the account works :  Supabase doesn't merely  market a database —it markets an  identity around building .

prompt: What do you know about Supabase (https://supabase.com/)?
answer:
is essentially a  backend-as-a-service built around PostgreSQL . It gives you the pieces you'd normally have to assemble yourself to build a modern web or mobile application's backend.
The core idea
Instead of setting up:
PostgreSQL + authentication server + file storage + APIs + realtime infrastructure + backend functions
you can create a Supabase project and get most of that as one integrated platform.
Each project includes a full PostgreSQL database, rather than a proprietary database abstraction.
The major pieces are:
• Postgres  — relational database, SQL, indexes, foreign keys, extensions, etc.
• Auth  — email/password, passwordless, OAuth and other authentication flows.
• Row Level Security (RLS)  — database-level policies controlling which users can access which rows .
• Storage  — files such as images, videos and documents, integrated with Postgres/RLS.
• Realtime  — subscribe to database changes and build synchronized/multiplayer experiences.
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript/Deno functions for custom backend logic and webhooks.
• Data APIs  — automatically generated APIs for your database.
• Vector/AI capabilities  — store and search embeddings and build AI/RAG  applications.
• Cron, queues and other Postgres extensions/tools  for more advanced backend workloads.
A simple example
Imagine you're building a SaaS application.
Your database might look like:
users
You could create those tables in Supabase, then write an RLS policy such as:
A user can SELECT a project
Your frontend can then query the database through Supabase's client library without you necessarily building a conventional REST/GraphQL backend yourself.
The important part is that  RLS is enforced at the database level , rather than relying purely on frontend code to decide what a user is allowed to see.
For example:
const  {  data  }  =  await  supabase   .from ( "projects" )   .select ( "*" )
The query can be made directly from your application, while Postgres/RLS determines which rows that particular user is actually permitted to receive.
Where Supabase gets particularly interesting
1. It's Postgres-first
This is probably the biggest distinction from something like Firebase.
With Supabase, you're dealing with  real PostgreSQL . You can use SQL, relational modeling, transactions, foreign keys, indexes, views, functions, extensions, etc.
That makes it attractive if you expect your application's data model to become sophisticated.
2. Auth + database + RLS fit together extremely well
This is arguably Supabase's killer combination.
You authenticate someone:
Alice → signs in
That lets you push a surprisingly large amount of authorization logic into PostgreSQL.
3. You can add backend code when you need it
You aren't limited to database queries.
Supabase Edge Functions let you write server-side TypeScript functions running on a Deno-compatible runtime. They're particularly useful for things like webhooks, Stripe integrations, AI calls, emails and custom APIs.
For example:
Browser
And authenticated Edge Functions can work with the caller's Supabase identity/RLS context.
4. It's increasingly AI-oriented
Supabase has become particularly popular in the AI application ecosystem.
A typical AI application might use:
Next.js
The platform explicitly supports vector embeddings alongside its database, APIs, auth, storage and functions.
Supabase vs Firebase
A rough mental model:

Supabase's open-source/self-hostable nature is an important part of its philosophy: its site explicitly emphasizes being able to inspect, contribute to and self-host the platform.
One thing I'd be careful about
Supabase makes it  very easy to get started , but that can actually make architectural mistakes easy too.
The biggest things I'd pay attention to are:
• RLS policies
• database indexes
• connection pooling
• migrations/schema management
• keeping privileged keys off the client
• designing authorization correctly
• understanding what should  run in Edge Functions vs. directly against Postgres
• avoiding putting all application logic into ad-hoc database queries
In particular,  never treat RLS as optional once your client can access data directly . Supabase's own security guidance recommends protecting exposed tables with RLS and giving each role only the privileges it needs.
My overall take
Supabase is one of the more compelling choices if you're building:
• a SaaS application
• a startup MVP
• a web/mobile app
• an internal tool
• an AI/RAG application
• a marketplace
• a collaborative/realtime application
• anything where you want  Postgres without having to operate Postgres infrastructure yourself
Its sweet spot is basically:
"I want a serious relational database and backend, but I don't want to spend the first month building backend infrastructure."
And  unlike some BaaS products, you're not giving up PostgreSQL to get that convenience.
If you're considering Supabase for a  specific project , tell me what you're building and your stack ( e.g. Next.js, React Native, Python, etc.). I can explain exactly how I'd structure the Supabase database, Auth, RLS, Storage and backend for it.

prompt: What do you know about Supabase (@supabase on X/Twitter)?
answer:
is  one of the  more interesting companies  in the modern  developer-tools / backend -as-a -service space. If  you know it  mainly from  @supabase on X , the short version  is:
Supabase is essentially “Postgres + the backend infrastructure most applications need,” wrapped in a very developer-friendly platform.
Its official positioning is a  Postgres development platform , and every project gets a full PostgreSQL database rather than a proprietary database abstraction.
What Supabase actually gives you
A typical Supabase project can include:
• Postgres  — a full relational  PostgreSQL database, including  extensions such as pgvector , PostGIS, and  pg_cron .
• Authentication  — email/password, magic  links, OAuth/social  login, MFA, SSO , etc.
• Row Level Security  (RLS)  — PostgreSQL-native authorization  policies that can  control which rows  each user can  access or modify . This is arguably  one of Supabase's  most important differentiators .
• Storage  — object/file storage  integrated with the  database and RLS .
• Realtime  — subscribe to database  changes and synchronize  state between clients .
• Edge Functions  — server-side Type Script functions running  on Supabase's globally  distributed edge runtime .
• APIs  — APIs are generated  around your database , so you can  go from a  schema to an  application backend very  quickly.
• AI/vector infrastructure  — PostgreSQL +  pgvector  makes it particularly  attractive for AI  applications that need  embeddings, retrieval,  metadata, and conventional  relational data together .
• CLI, local development  and self-hosting  — the project is  open source and  designed to be  developed locally and , where appropriate, self -hosted.
So instead of  assembling:
Postgres + Auth0/Clerk  + S3 + WebSockets + API  server + serverless functions  + database tooling
you can get  most of that  from one platform .
Why developers like  it
The really clever  part of Supabase  is that  Postgres remains the  center of gravity .
That's different from  a platform where  the database is  an implementation detail  behind a proprietary  API. With Supabase , you can use  SQL , PostgreSQL extensions,  foreign keys, indexes , functions, triggers, RLS , etc. Your application  is still fundamentally  sitting on Postgres .
That has a  few big advantages :
1. It is  familiar to serious  backend developers.
You don't have  to learn an  entirely new database  paradigm.
2. You can  start ridiculously quickly .
For a small  SaaS, for example , you could create :
users
add RLS policies , authentication, and APIs ,  and have a  functioning backend without  first building a  conventional API server .
3. It scales  conceptually with the  application.
You can begin  with simple CRUD  and eventually use  sophisticated  PostgreSQL functionality  rather than immediately  replacing your database  architecture.
4. It works  extremely well with  AI-assisted development .
This is becoming  a major part  of Supabase's positioning . Their current tooling  explicitly targets  AI builders and  agentic development, and  Supabase has added  things such as  MCP and platform  APIs.
The AI angle  is particularly interesting
This is where  I think  @supabase's presence on  X makes more  sense .
Supabase has moved  beyond being merely  "Firebase but Postgres ."
They're increasingly  positioning themselves  as  infrastructure for AI -generated applications .
An AI coding  agent can create  a Supabase project , create tables, write  SQL/RLS policies , add authentication, create  functions, and interact  with  the backend programmatically .
They even launched Supabase for Platforms , which allows another  company to programmatically  provision Supabase backends  for its own  users. Supabase specifically  calls out AI  builders and platforms  as a major  use case .
That's strategically important  because the future  could look something  like:
Human:  "Build me a  marketplace for vintage  watches."
AI agent:  creates the frontend  → creates Supabase project  → creates schema → creates  RLS → creates auth  → creates storage → creates  APIs → deploys functions .
Supabase  wants to be  the  backend substrate underneath  that entire process .

prompt: What do you know about https://supabase.com/ and @supabase on X/Twitter?
answer:
Yes. I looked at both the current
and the
. Supabase is one of the more interesting developer platforms to understand right now, particularly because it sits at the intersection of
Postgres, backend-as-a-service, open source, and AI-assisted development
.
What Supabase actually is
The simplest description is:
Supabase is a developer platform built around a real Postgres database.
Instead of giving you only a database, it gives you most of the backend infrastructure you'd normally have to assemble yourself:
• Postgres database  — a full PostgreSQL database, rather than a proprietary database abstraction.
• Authentication  — accounts, login, OAuth, sessions, etc.
• Row Level Security (RLS)  — database-level rules controlling which users can access which rows.
• Storage  — files, images, videos, etc.
• Realtime  — push database changes to clients in real time.
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript/Deno functions.
• Data APIs  — automatically generated APIs over your database.
• Vector/pgvector capabilities  — useful for embeddings, semantic search and AI applications.
That's all integrated into one platform.
A useful mental model is:
Firebase → but PostgreSQL-first and much more open-source-oriented.
Supabase itself explicitly says it isn't simply trying to reproduce Firebase: its fundamental architectural choice is to put
Postgres at the center
.
Why Postgres is such a big deal
This is probably the most important thing to understand about Supabase. When you create a Supabase project, you aren't getting some simplified database that happens to look like SQL. You get an actual Postgres database, with access to PostgreSQL's capabilities and ecosystem.
That gives developers something like:
Your application
And that distinction matters. If your application becomes sophisticated, you can drop down into SQL, PostgreSQL extensions, indexes, functions, transactions, foreign keys, etc., rather than eventually discovering that your BaaS has hidden the database from you. Supabase also emphasizes portability: its Postgres databases can be migrated to other Postgres environments rather than locking your data into a proprietary database format.
The open-source angle
This is another major part of the company's identity. Supabase says it has been
open source from day one
, and its architecture uses a collection of open-source projects rather than building a completely proprietary backend stack.
For example, its architecture incorporates:
• PostgreSQL
• PostgREST
• GoTrue
• Realtime/Phoenix
• pgvector
• Deno
• imgproxy
• and other open-source components.
Supabase reported passing
100,000 GitHub stars
in early 2026, which is a pretty extraordinary indicator of developer interest for infrastructure software.
That's important because Supabase isn't merely selling a hosted API. There's a substantial ecosystem and community around the underlying technology.
Why developers seem to love it
The biggest advantage is
developer velocity
. Imagine you're building a SaaS product. Without something like Supabase, you might need:
Frontend
With Supabase, a lot of that becomes:
Frontend
And you can progressively add the other capabilities as necessary. The company's current positioning—"build in a weekend, scale to millions"—is essentially selling that reduction in infrastructure complexity.
And this is where AI gets interesting
I think this is one of the most important things happening around Supabase. Supabase has become extremely compatible with the
AI-assisted coding / "vibe coding" ecosystem
. For example, its own current site highlights integrations and templates involving:
• Next.js
• Vercel
• OpenAI
• LangChain
• AI chatbots
• Expo/React Native
• Stripe
It also showcases Lovable as a customer, describing Supabase as the backend powering millions of AI-generated applications.
This makes strategic sense. AI can generate frontend code extremely quickly. But generated applications still need:
users + database + permissions + files + APIs + server-side logic.
That's precisely where Supabase fits. So there's an interesting flywheel:
AI makes it easier to create software → more people need instant backends → Supabase makes those backends easy → more people build software → Supabase gets more developers.
That's potentially much bigger than the traditional "Firebase alternative" positioning.
What @supabase on X is like
The X account is very much an extension of that developer-first identity. The account currently has roughly
200K followers
and describes itself as "The Postgres development platform."
The content tends to revolve around:
• product launches
• new Supabase features
• Postgres
• AI
• developer tools
• open source
• tutorials/examples
• community projects
• developer humor
• startup/build-in-public culture
• integrations with other developer tools
And importantly,
the community itself is a significant part of the marketing engine
. Supabase's own site prominently surfaces positive posts from developers about things like its developer experience, Advisors, Edge Functions, MCP, documentation and speed of getting applications running.
There's a recognizable pattern:
"I tried Supabase and suddenly my backend just works."
That's a very powerful product story.
MCP is particularly interesting
One thing I'd pay attention to if you're studying where Supabase is heading is
MCP (Model Context Protocol)
. Supabase is positioning its tooling so AI coding agents can interact with a project's database and infrastructure. That's significant because the traditional workflow is:
Human
The emerging workflow is:
Human
In other words, Supabase isn't only trying to be the backend for developers. It increasingly has an opportunity to become the
backend that AI agents can operate on behalf of developers
. That's a much more interesting strategic position.
Where I would put Supabase competitively
I'd think about the landscape roughly like this:
Platform
Core philosophy
Supabase
Postgres + open-source backend platform
Firebase
Google's integrated app backend
Vercel
Frontend/web deployment + increasingly full-stack infrastructure
Neon
Serverless Postgres
PlanetScale
Cloud database infrastructure
AWS
Extremely broad infrastructure platform
Convex
Reactive backend/database designed around application development
Supabase's differentiation isn't simply "we have a database." It's:
"You get the power of Postgres without having to assemble and operate the surrounding backend yourself."
That's a very compelling proposition.
One thing I'd be careful about
"Supabase is open source" can be slightly misleading if interpreted as
everything about the commercial Supabase service is completely equivalent to self-hosting the entire SaaS platform
. The underlying components and much of the platform are open source, and Supabase explicitly supports self-hosting. But the managed Supabase service is still a commercial cloud product with operational infrastructure, billing, support, reliability, etc.
So I'd distinguish:
Open-source technology + commercial managed cloud.
That's a very common and sensible infrastructure-business model.
My overall take
If you're trying to understand
why Supabase has become so prominent
, I'd boil it down to five things:
Postgres is an excellent foundation.
They turned a complicated backend stack into a remarkably simple developer experience.
They embraced open source and developer community unusually aggressively.
They arrived at exactly the right time for startups and AI-assisted software development.
They're increasingly positioning themselves as infrastructure that AI coding agents can directly manipulate.
The last two are, IMO, the most strategically interesting. Supabase started looking like
"the open-source Firebase alternative."
Today, I think the more interesting description is:
Supabase is trying to become the default Postgres-powered backend for the next generation of software—especially software increasingly created with AI.
And its presence on X reflects that strategy very clearly:
product + developers + open source + AI + community
, rather than traditional enterprise-software marketing.
If you're asking because you're considering
using Supabase, investing in/competing with Supabase, building a business on it, or studying their X/content strategy
, I can go considerably deeper into any of those angles.

prompt: What do you know about Supabase (https://supabase.com/, @supabase on X/Twitter)?
answer:
is  a developer platform built around  PostgreSQL . The simplest way to think about it  is:
“Postgres + the backend services you normally have to build around it, packaged into one developer-friendly platform.”
What Supabase actually provides
Every Supabase project gives you a full PostgreSQL database rather than a proprietary database abstraction. Around that database, Supabase provides:
• Postgres database  — relational database with SQL, extensions, indexes, triggers, functions, etc.
• Authentication  — email/password, OAuth, magic links, passkeys, and other authentication flows.
• Row Level Security (RLS)  — PostgreSQL policies that let you control exactly which rows a user can access.
• Auto-generated APIs  — REST APIs generated from your database schema.
• Realtime  — subscribe to database changes and build collaborative/live applications.
• Storage  — files such as images, videos and documents, with access controls.
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript functions for backend logic.

prompt: What do you know about Supabase?
answer:
is an open-source backend-as -a-service (BaaS) platform built around  PostgreSQL . It’s often described as an open-source alternative to Firebase , but the PostgreSQL foundation makes it particularly attractive if you want a traditional relational database and SQL.
What  Supabase provides
• PostgreSQL database  — a full Postgres database, with SQL, relationships, indexes, views, functions, triggers, extensions,  etc.
• Authentication  — email/password, magic links, OAuth providers, social login, and more.
• Row Level Security (RLS)  — PostgreSQL policies that let you control exactly which rows users can read or modify.
• Storage  — object /file storage for images, videos, documents, etc., with access policies.
• Realtime  — subscribe to database changes and broadcast events  to clients.
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript functions running close to users.
• Auto-generated APIs  — REST APIs are generated from your database schema, and Supabase also supports  GraphQL through its ecosystem.
• Local development  — a CLI and Docker-based local stack let you develop against  a local Supabase instance.
• Dashboard  — web UI for managing your  database, auth, storage, logs, SQL, and other services.
Why developers like it
The biggest selling point is that  you aren't learning a proprietary database abstraction . You're working with PostgreSQL.
For example, your application might look conceptually like:
React / Next.js / Flutter / iOS / Android
That means you can write normal SQL, use foreign keys and transactions, create database functions, and apply PostgreSQL's mature  ecosystem.
The  RLS + Auth combination  is especially powerful. You can express something like:
"A user can read only rows belonging to their organization."
directly as a PostgreSQL security policy rather  than relying entirely on application code.
Where it fits well
Supabase is particularly compelling for:
• SaaS applications
• Internal tools
• MVPs and startups
• Mobile apps
• CRUD-heavy applications
• Multi- tenant applications
• Applications where relational data matters
• Products that need realtime features
• Teams that already know SQL /Postgres

organizations

prompt: What do you know about https://supabase.com/?
answer:
is essentially a  managed backend platform built around PostgreSQL . Its big selling point is that you can get most of the  infrastructure needed for a modern web/mobile app without building each backend component yourself.
What you get
A Supabase project currently bundles:
• PostgreSQL database  — a real Postgres database, rather than a proprietary database abstraction.
• Authentication  — email/password, social login, SSO, sessions/JWTs, etc.
• Row Level Security (RLS)  — database-level policies controlling which users can read/write which rows. This is one of Supabase's most important features.
• Storage  — object/file storage for images, videos, documents, uploads, etc.
• Realtime  — subscribe to database changes and build collaborative/live applications.
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript/Deno functions for APIs,  webhooks, integrations, AI calls, payments, background-ish tasks, etc.
• Vector/pgvector support  — useful for  embeddings, semantic search and AI/RAG applications.
• Auto-generated APIs  — you can interact with your database through APIs/client libraries rather than writing a conventional backend for every CRUD operation.
The architecture is interesting because these aren't really separate products glued together:  Postgres is the center of the system , with Auth, Storage, Realtime, Functions and APIs working around it.
Why developers like it
Imagine you're building a SaaS application.
Without Supabase, you might need:
PostgreSQL + database hosting + authentication provider + object storage + API server + realtime infrastructure + secrets management + deployment infrastructure
With Supabase, you can start with essentially:
Supabase + your frontend
For example, a React application can directly query a table through the Supabase client:
const  {  data  }  = await  supabase .from ( 'todos' ) .select ( '*' )
The really powerful part is that  RLS can determine what that query is actually allowed to return . So instead of relying entirely on your application server to remember "Alice can only see  Alice's records," you can enforce that rule at the database layer.
Where it gets particularly interesting
Supabase is increasingly attractive for  AI applications  too.
For example, you could build:
Next.js / React
The Edge Functions can act as your secure server-side layer for things like calling an LLM, processing webhooks, or integrating Stripe.
Is it like Firebase?
Yes, but the underlying philosophy is quite different.

Supabase explicitly positions itself as open source and says you can self-host it, which can reduce concerns about vendor lock-in.
The  important caveat
Supabase isn't magic.  RLS/security architecture is something you need to understand properly.
The convenience of being able to access Post gres directly from a frontend is fantastic, but it means you have to design your database policies correctly. Supabase itself recommends protecting exposed tables with RLS.
Also, Edge Functions aren't intended to replace arbitrary long-running backend workers; Supabase notes that cold starts can occur and recommends moving heavy/long-running jobs to appropriate background infrastructure.
My overall take
If you're building a  new web app, SaaS, internal tool, mobile app, AI application, or prototype , Supabase is  one of the platforms I'd seriously consider today.
Its strongest combination is:
Postgres + Auth + RLS + Storage + APIs + Realtime + serverless functions + open-source/self-hostable architecture.
That's a surprisingly large portion of a backend in one platform.
If you tell me  what you're thinking of building , I can also explain exactly  how I'd architect it with Supabase —including the database schema, Auth/RLS model, API structure, Edge Functions, and what  not  to put in Supabase.

prompt: What do you know about Supabase (https://supabase.com/)?
answer:
is essentially a
backend-as-a-service built around PostgreSQL
. It gives you a production-ready backend without requiring you to build and operate all the infrastructure yourself.
The simple mental model
Think of it as:
Postgres + Auth + APIs + Storage + Realtime + server-side functions, packaged together.
The important distinction is that Supabase isn't hiding the database behind a proprietary NoSQL abstraction. Every project gets a
full PostgreSQL database
, and the other services integrate closely with it.
What you get
• PostgreSQL  — relational database, SQL, foreign keys, indexes, extensions, functions, triggers, etc.
• Authentication  — email/password, passwordless, OAuth, mobile authentication, and user management.
• Row Level Security (RLS)  — database-level policies that determine which users can read/write which rows.
• Auto-generated APIs  — interact with your Postgres data through REST and client libraries; GraphQL is also available.
• Storage  — files such as images, videos, PDFs, etc., with access controlled through policies.
• Realtime  — subscribe to database changes and synchronize state between clients.
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript/Deno functions for things like webhooks, APIs, integrations, and AI calls.
• Vector/AI capabilities  — store and search embeddings alongside your relational data.
• Cron and Queues  — useful for scheduled and background work.
• CLI + local development  — you can run much of the stack locally rather than being completely dependent on the hosted service.
Why developers like it
The biggest advantage is
how much you can build without creating a traditional backend
. For example, imagine you're building a SaaS application:
React / Next.js frontend
A user signs up → Supabase Auth creates/manages the identity → your application stores their data in Postgres → RLS ensures they can only access their own data → Storage handles their files → Realtime can push changes to their browser. You can do all of that without maintaining your own authentication server, API server, database server, file server, etc.
RLS is particularly important
One of Supabase's most powerful—and initially confusing—features is
Row Level Security
. Instead of relying entirely on something like:
request → backend → "is this user allowed?" → database
you can put authorization rules directly into PostgreSQL:
request
For example, conceptually:
create policy "Users can view their own profiles"
That means the database itself enforces the rule. Supabase specifically recommends RLS when exposing database access through its Data APIs.
This is one reason Supabase can be very attractive for applications where
security and multi-tenancy
matter.
What are Edge Functions?
They're Supabase's server-side execution environment. You might use one for:
• Stripe webhooks
• Calling an external API while keeping a secret key private
• Sending an email
• AI/LLM calls
• Payment processing
• Custom API endpoints
• Scheduled/background operations
They're TypeScript functions running on Supabase's Deno-based edge runtime.
For example:
Browser
Supabase also provides mechanisms for authenticating Edge Function calls and integrating them with RLS.
Supabase vs Firebase
This is probably the most common comparison.
Supabase
Firebase
Primary database
PostgreSQL
Firestore
Data model
Relational
Document
SQL
Yes
No
RLS
Yes
Security Rules
Auth
Yes
Yes
File storage
Yes
Yes
Realtime
Yes
Yes
Serverless functions
Yes
Yes
Open source
Much more open/self-hostable
No equivalent full-stack open-source offering
Existing Postgres ecosystem
Excellent
N/A
If your application's data naturally looks relational—users → organizations → projects → memberships → invoices → subscriptions—
Supabase/Postgres is particularly compelling
. If you're deeply invested in Google's ecosystem or Firebase's client-first architecture, Firebase can still make sense.
One of its biggest strengths: you're not trapped in a proprietary database
This is a meaningful difference. Your underlying database is PostgreSQL, so you're working with a widely used database technology rather than learning a completely proprietary data model. Supabase also explicitly supports self-hosting.
That gives you a potential migration path:
Supabase
rather than:
proprietary backend
Of course, migrating an entire application still isn't trivial—Auth, Storage, Functions, RLS, etc. create additional coupling—but the Postgres foundation is a substantial advantage.
Where I would use Supabase
I'd seriously consider it for:
• SaaS products
• Internal business applications
• Dashboards/admin systems
• Marketplaces
• Mobile apps
• AI applications
• CRUD-heavy applications
• Multi-tenant B2B software
• MVPs that may eventually become production systems
• Applications where you want SQL without managing PostgreSQL yourself
It's especially interesting for
AI applications
because you can keep application data and vector embeddings in the same Postgres ecosystem, while Edge Functions can orchestrate calls to external AI APIs. Supabase itself now positions AI/vector functionality prominently.
The caveats
It's not magic. The biggest things I'd watch are:
• RLS complexity  — powerful, but poorly designed policies can become difficult to reason about.
• Database architecture still matters  — Supabase doesn't eliminate SQL, indexing, transactions, migrations, connection pooling, etc.
• Edge Functions aren't a replacement for arbitrary backend infrastructure  — long-running/heavy workloads may need dedicated workers or other infrastructure.
• You can still create vendor coupling  through Supabase Auth, Storage, Realtime, Functions, etc.
• Costs need to be modeled at scale  rather than assuming the initial free/cheap tier represents production economics.
But overall, I'd describe Supabase as
one of the more developer-friendly ways to get a serious PostgreSQL-backed application running quickly
. If you're asking because you're considering using Supabase for a
specific project
, tell me what you're building and I can map out exactly which Supabase components I'd use, what the architecture would look like, and where I'd
not
use Supabase.

answer:
Yes. I looked at both  the current
and the
.
What Supabase is
is essentially a  developer platform built around PostgreSQL .
The easiest mental model is:
“Firebase, but PostgreSQL-first and much more open.”
A Supabase project gives you a real Postgres database rather than hiding the database behind a proprietary abstraction. Around that database, Supabase provides:
• Database  — full PostgreSQL, including SQL, extensions, indexes, functions, triggers, etc.
• Authentication  — sign-up/login , OAuth, sessions, and authorization.
• Storage  — files such as images, videos, documents, etc.
• Realtime  — subscriptions to database  changes and realtime communication.
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript/Deno functions.
• Data APIs  — automatically generated APIs over your database.
• Vector/AI capabilities  — including  pgvector  for embeddings and AI applications.
• Dashboard and tooling  — SQL editor , table editor, security advisors, CLI, migrations, branching, etc.
That's not just marketing language: their current architecture explicitly treats  Postgres as the core , with Auth, Storage, Realtime, Functions and APIs surrounding it.
Why developers like it
The important strategic choice is  Postgres instead of a proprietary database abstraction .
For example, you can start with:
Your app
and directly use SQL:
select *
You aren't learning a completely new database model.
Supabase also automatically generates a REST API from your database schema, so a table can effectively become an API without you having to write the CRUD backend yourself.
And because it is built around PostgreSQL, you get things like  foreign keys, transactions, SQL, JSON, extensions, full-text search, PostGIS, pgvector , etc.
That's a pretty powerful combination for startups and small teams.
The “open source” part is important
Supabase isn't simply a proprietary SaaS company that happens to use Postgres.
A substantial portion of its platform is open source, and Supabase explicitly supports  self-hosting . Their architecture documentation describes the individual services and their open-source foundations.
That gives you an interesting escape hatch:
Hosted Supabase
Your application
versus:

Your application
So there is considerably less vendor lock-in than with a completely proprietary backend platform.
And @supabase on X?
The account is  @supabase , the official Supabase account. X currently lists it as a software company account with roughly  202K followers .
Their X presence is particularly interesting because Supabase has built a fairly strong  developer-community brand , rather than behaving like a conventional enterprise database vendor.
The themes you see around the brand are generally:
• developers building projects
• Postgres tips
• new product/features
• AI and agents
• integrations
• open-source projects
• developer memes/content
• customer/build stories
• community projects
• tutorials and demos
In other words,  Supabase is as much a developer ecosystem/brand as it is a backend product.
That's a big part of why it has become prominent among indie hackers, startups, AI developers, and modern web developers.
The AI angle is particularly interesting
Supabase has been pushing increasingly hard into  AI-native application development .
The underlying architecture makes a lot of sense for this:
AI model
So you can keep your application's:
• users
• permissions
• relational data
• documents
• embeddings
• application state
in one ecosystem.
Supabase's current documentation explicitly positions AI, vectors and embeddings as a major use case, alongside newer AI-oriented tooling such as MCP.
One thing worth knowing about the company
Supabase has become  much more than “an open-source Firebase alternative.”
That was the original/easiest way to understand it, but I think the  more accurate description today is:
A Postgres-centric application development platform.
The distinction matters.
Firebase essentially starts from Google's infrastructure and gives you a  managed application backend.
Supabase starts from  Postgres  and builds an entire developer platform around it.
That makes Supabase particularly attractive if you want the convenience  of a BaaS but don't want to give up the power and familiarity of SQL/Postgres.
One recent wrinkle
There was also a  significant access issue involving Supabase in  India in February 2026 , where some ISPs reportedly blocked access to Supabase following a government order. Supabase acknowledged the problem publicly and said  its infrastructure itself remained operational.
That's an interesting reminder that although Supabase is open source and self-hostable,  using Supabase Cloud still introduces cloud-provider/infrastructure dependency . Self-hosting is the escape hatch, but it isn't necessarily operationally equivalent  to using their managed service.

prompt: What do you know about Supabase (https://supabase.com/, @supabase on X/Twitter)?
answer:
is one of the most popular  developer-focused backend platforms , essentially giving you a production-ready backend centered around  PostgreSQL .
What Supabase actually is
The simplest mental model is:
Supabase = hosted Postgres + Auth + APIs + Storage + Realtime + server-side functions + developer tooling.
Unlike some backend-as-a-service platforms that hide the underlying database behind their own abstractions,  each Supabase project gives you a full PostgreSQL database . You can use SQL, PostgreSQL extensions, foreign keys, views, functions, triggers, etc.
Around that database, Supabase provides:
• PostgreSQL database  — relational data, SQL, indexes, constraints, extensions, etc.
• Authentication  — email /password, passwordless, OAuth/social login, SSO, JWTs, etc.
• Row Level Security (RLS)  — PostgreSQL  policies that let you control exactly which rows a user can access.
• Auto-generated APIs  — REST APIs generated from your database schema.
• Storage  — files such as images, videos and documents, with access policies integrated with Postgres /RLS.
• Realtime  — subscribe to database changes and synchronize state between clients.
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript/JavaScript functions running  on Deno, useful for webhooks, custom APIs, AI calls, privileged operations, etc.
• Vector/AI capabilities  — store, index and search embeddings in Post gres.
• Cron and queues  — increasingly useful for background jobs and scheduled workloads.
• Local development / CLI / migrations  — allowing you to develop against  a local Supabase environment rather than being completely dependent on the hosted service.
Why developers like it
The really compelling part is the  integration .
Imagine you're building a SaaS application. Traditionally you might need:
PostgreSQL
With Supabase, those pieces are designed to work together around the same Postgres database.
For example:
React / Next.js / Flutter / mobile app
That makes it particularly attractive for  startups, SaaS applications, internal tools, mobile apps, prototypes, AI applications and products where you want to move quickly without building backend infrastructure from scratch .
Supabase itself currently positions the platform around going from prototype to very large-scale applications, and its site highlights customers such as Lovable, Chatbase and others.
The really important feature: PostgreSQL + RLS
If you're evaluating Supabase technically, I'd pay particular attention to  Row Level Security .
For example, suppose you have:
messages
You can establish a database policy conceptually like:
CREATE POLICY "Users can see their own messages"
Now access control is enforced  at the database layer , rather than relying solely on your frontend or API code.
That's one of Supabase's biggest architectural advantages: authentication and authorization can be tightly connected to PostgreSQL itself. Supabase Auth issues JWTs, and those identities can be used by PostgreSQL RLS policies.

If you're comfortable with SQL,  Supabase often feels much more natural than Firebase .
Is it actually "serverless"?
Sort of—but I'd describe it more precisely as a  managed backend platform .
You don't need to administer a PostgreSQL server, configure replication, build authentication infrastructure, or operate your own API layer for many applications.
But underneath, you're still dealing with very real infrastructure: PostgreSQL, networking, connection pooling, compute, storage, backups, etc.
Supabase provides a managed platform around those things.
And importantly, you're not just talking to some proprietary black-box database. Supabase emphasizes PostgreSQL portability and says you can migrate existing Postgres databases into it or away from it.
Where it gets especially interesting in 2026
Supabase has become increasingly relevant to the  AI-app ecosystem .
A typical AI application might need:
Users
Then Edge Functions can handle things such as model calls, webhooks, document processing or other server-side logic. Supabase explicitly supports vector embeddings alongside its database platform.
This is one reason it shows up so frequently in modern  AI-generated/vibe-coded applications : you can give an AI coding agent a fairly complete backend environment without having to design and deploy every backend subsystem yourself.
What I would
not
use it for
Supabase isn't automatically the right answer for everything.
I'd be more cautious if you need:
• Extremely specialized database infrastructure.
• Complex distributed systems beyond what Postgres is suited for.
• Very unusual networking/infrastructure requirements.
• A backend whose architecture is intentionally split across many specialized services.
• Extremely high-throughput workloads where you need fine-grained control over every infrastructure layer.
And RLS, while extremely powerful, introduces its own learning curve.  A Supabase application can absolutely have serious security vulnerabilities if its RLS policies are poorly designed.  The fact that Supabase makes RLS easy to use doesn't mean you can skip learning PostgreSQL authorization.
Supabase does have formal security/compliance programs, including SOC 2 Type 2, ISO 27001 and HIPAA-related offerings.
My short take
If I were explaining Supabase to a developer in one sentence:
Supabase is a PostgreSQL-first backend platform that lets you build most of a modern application's backend without having to build and operate the backend infrastructure yourself.
And its strategic advantage is pretty clear:
Postgres is the foundation, rather than an implementation detail.
That's a big deal. It means you get the convenience of a BaaS while retaining much of the flexibility and familiarity of a conventional SQL backend.
If you're asking because you're  considering  using Supabase for a particular product , tell me what you're building. I can also break down  Supabase's architecture, pricing/cost model, security/RLS, Supabase vs Firebase/Neon/PlanetScale, or whether I'd choose it for your specific application .

prompt: What do you know about Supabase?
answer:
is an open-source backend-as-a-service platform built around
PostgreSQL
. It’s often described as a “Firebase alternative,” but its architecture is quite different because Postgres is the core rather than a proprietary NoSQL database.
What Supabase provides
• Postgres database  — a full PostgreSQL database, including SQL, joins, indexes, extensions, views, functions, triggers, etc.
• Authentication  — email/password, magic links, OAuth providers, and other auth flows.
• Auto-generated APIs  — REST APIs and database access based on your schema.
• Realtime  — subscribe to database changes and build realtime applications.
• Storage  — object/file storage with access policies.
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript functions for backend logic.
• Row Level Security (RLS)  — PostgreSQL's security policies can be used to control exactly which rows users can access.
• Dashboard and tooling  — SQL editor, database management, logs, authentication management, storage management, and more.
• Self-hosting  — much of the platform is open source, so you can run Supabase yourself rather than using the hosted service.
Why developers like it
The big selling point is that you get a surprisingly complete backend
without giving up PostgreSQL
. For example, you might create:
users
Then use RLS policies to say things like:
A user can read tasks only when they belong to a project that the user has access to.
That authorization logic can live close to the database instead of requiring every API endpoint to implement it independently.
Supabase vs. Firebase
A simplified comparison:

If you're comfortable with SQL, Supabase is particularly attractive.
Where it shines
I'd consider Supabase a strong choice for:
• SaaS applications
• Web apps
• Mobile app backends
• Internal tools
• Dashboards
• Marketplaces
• CRUD-heavy applications
• Apps that need relational data
• MVPs that may eventually become substantial products
It's also useful when you want to move quickly: instead of building a database, auth system, API layer, storage system, and realtime infrastructure separately, you get most of that as one integrated platform.
The important caveat
Supabase isn't simply “a database with an API.” Once you use
RLS, authentication, database functions, triggers, realtime, storage policies, and Edge Functions
, you're building an architecture with several interacting pieces. The biggest things I'd pay attention to in a serious Supabase project are:
RLS design  — security mistakes here can expose data.
Database schema and indexes  — Postgres gives you enormous flexibility, but you still need to design it well.
Connection management  — particularly for serverless workloads.
Migration discipline  — treat your database schema as code.
Service-role keys  — never expose privileged credentials to clients.
Vendor dependence  — although the underlying technologies are portable, moving an entire Supabase application isn't necessarily frictionless.
If you're considering Supabase for a
specific project
, tell me what you're building and your frontend/backend stack (e.g. Next.js, React Native, Python, etc.). I can tell you whether I'd choose Supabase and what architecture I'd use.

prompt: What do you know about https://supabase.com/?
answer:
is essentially a backend-as-a -service built around  PostgreSQL . If you're building  a web or  mobile  application, it can  provide most of  the backend infrastructure  you'd otherwise have  to assemble yourself .
What Supabase gives you
• PostgreSQL database  — Every project gets  a real Postgres  database, rather than  a proprietary database  abstraction. You can  use SQL directly , relationships, indexes , extensions, triggers,  etc.
• Authentication  — Email/password, passwordless  authentication, OAuth providers , mobile authentication,  sessions, etc.
• Row Level Security  (RLS)  — One of its  most important features . You can define  database policies such  as "users can  only read rows  belonging to their  account."
• Storage  — Object/file storage  for images, videos , documents,  uploads, and  other large files , integrated with your  database and RLS  policies.
• Realtime  — Clients can subscribe  to database changes  and synchronize state  in realtime, useful  for chat, collaborative  applications, dashboards , multiplayer features,  etc.
• Edge Functions  — Server-side TypeScript /Deno functions for  APIs, webhooks, payments , AI calls, scheduled -ish workloads, and  other backend logic .
• Auto-generated APIs  — Your database can  be accessed through  generated APIs, so  you don't necessarily  need to write  a conventional REST  backend for every  CRUD operation .
• Vector/AI capabilities  — It supports storing  and searching vector  embeddings, making it  useful for RAG  and AI applications .
• CLI + local development  + self-hosting  — Supabase is open  source and can  be run locally /self-hosted, which  gives you considerably  more control than  a purely proprietary  backend platform.
The simplest way  to think about  it
Imagine you're building  a SaaS application :
Your React / Next.js / Flutter App
Instead of building :
Postgres
you can  get most of  that from one  platform.
Why developers like  it
The particularly nice  part is that Postgres remains the  center of the  system . You're not learning  an entirely new  database model.
For example, you  could have:
users
Then use SQL , foreign keys, indexes , views, functions, RLS  policies, etc., just  as you would  with normal  PostgreSQL.
That's a major  difference from something  like Firebase/Firestore , where the database  model is fundamentally  different.
Where Supabase gets  particularly interesting
For  AI applications , it's become especially  compelling.
You can have :
User
Supabase itself explicitly  positions the platform  for AI builders  and provides database /vector capabilities alongside  Edge Functions.
The big thing  to understand: RLS
If you're considering  using Supabase seriously , I'd spend time  learning  Row Level Security .
For example, instead  of trusting your  application server to  enforce:
"Alice can only  see Alice's records ."
you can enforce  that rule  at the database  level .
That's extremely powerful , but it  also means a  badly designed RLS  policy can create  security problems. Supabase's  own documentation emphasizes  protecting exposed tables  with RLS and  giving each  role only the  privileges it needs .
Supabase vs Firebase , in one sentence
I'd characterize it  roughly as:
Firebase:  " Google's developer-friendly  backend platform built  around its own  managed services/database  model."
Supabase:  "An open-source , Postgres-centered backend  platform that gives  you database + auth  + storage + realtime +  functions + APIs."
If you're  comfortable with SQL /Postgres,  Supabase is usually  a very natural  fit .
And importantly, you're  not locked into  an opaque database  abstraction: Supabase says  each project is  a full PostgreSQL  database, and the  platform  can also be  self-hosted.

prompt: What do you know about Supabase (https://supabase.com/)?
answer:
is essentially a  backend-as-a-service built around PostgreSQL . The important distinction from something like Firebase is that Supabase gives you an actual  Postgres database rather than hiding the database behind a proprietary abstraction.
What you get
A Supabase project bundles several backend capabilities:
• PostgreSQL database  — a full Postgres instance, with SQL, relationships, extensions, indexes, views,  functions, etc.
• Authentication  — email/password, passwordless, OAuth/social login, SSO, JWT-based sessions, and user management.
• Row Level Security (RLS)  — Postgres policies that let you define precisely which rows a particular user can read/write. This is one of Supabase's most important architectural features.
• Auto-generated APIs  — APIs are generated around your database, so you can interact with tables without writing a conventional REST backend yourself.
• Storage  — object/file storage integrated with Postgres and RLS, useful for images, videos, documents, etc.
• Realtime  —  subscribe to database changes and build things like collaborative interfaces, live dashboards, chat, and multiplayer applications.
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript /Deno functions for custom backend logic, webhooks, third-party integrations, AI calls, payments, etc.
• Vector/AI functionality  — storage, indexing, and  searching of vector embeddings, allowing Postgres to participate in RAG/AI applications.
• Cron, queues, REST/GraphQL APIs and other Postgres extensions  are also part of the broader platform.
Why developers like it
The big attraction is  how much backend infrastructure you don't have to build yourself .
For example, a typical SaaS application might otherwise require:
Frontend
With Supabase, much of that becomes:
Frontend
That's particularly attractive for  startups, prototypes, internal tools, SaaS products, mobile apps, and AI applications  where you want to get a working product running quickly.
Supabase also emphasizes being  open source and self-hostable , which gives it a different philosophy from purely proprietary backend platforms.
The really interesting part: RLS
If you're evaluating Supabase seriously, I'd pay particular attention to  Postgres Row Level Security .
Imagine a  documents  table:
documents
You can create a database policy conceptually saying:
A logged-in user may only access documents where  owner_id = their user ID .
The database itself enforces that rule.
That means authorization isn't necessarily something you have to remember to implement in every API endpoint. Supabase's APIs and functions can operate within those Postgres policies.
This can make relatively simple applications  surprisingly secure and elegant , provided the RLS policies are designed correctly.
Where Supabase fits
I'd roughly think of the ecosystem like this:
If you want...
Supabase's position
Managed PostgreSQL
Excellent fit
Quick SaaS backend
Excellent fit
Auth + database together
Excellent fit
File storage
Good fit
Realtime applications
Good fit
AI/RAG applications
Increasingly strong fit
Highly custom backend architecture
Possible, but you may eventually want your own services
Firebase-style development
Strong alternative, especially if you prefer SQL/Postgres
Traditional backend + Postgres
Supabase can replace a lot of the infrastructure, but doesn't have to
One particularly nice thing is that you're  not really learning a proprietary database . Your underlying data is PostgreSQL, and Supabase provides multiple ways of connecting to it, including ordinary Postgres connection strings.
What I would be cautious about
Supabase isn't magic. The biggest things I'd think about before committing a production system are:
• RLS complexity  — powerful, but poorly designed policies can create security holes or become difficult to reason about.
• Vendor/platform coupling  — although Postgres is portable,  moving every Supabase-specific feature (Auth, Realtime, Storage, Edge Functions, etc.) elsewhere takes work.
• Serverless/edge architecture  — Edge Functions have cold starts and are intended  for relatively short-lived operations; heavy background work may need another architecture.
• Database architecture still matters  — Supabase doesn't eliminate the  need to understand indexes, transactions, query performance, connection pooling, migrations, etc.
• Costs at scale  — the economics need to be evaluated based on database  size, compute, bandwidth, storage, realtime traffic, and function usage rather than simply assuming it's inexpensive because the initial project is easy to create.
My overall take
Supabase is one of the more compelling choices if you want to build a modern application around PostgreSQL without spending weeks assembling backend infrastructure.
Its strongest proposition is  not merely "hosted Postgres." It's:
Postgres + authentication + authorization + APIs + storage + realtime + server-side functions, packaged into one developer experience.
And  because the underlying database is real PostgreSQL, you retain a lot more of the power and portability of the traditional relational-database ecosystem.
If you're considering Supabase  for a  specific project , tell me what you're building and your frontend/backend stack (e.g. Next.js, React Native, Python, Flutter, etc.). I can map out  exactly how I'd architect it with Supabase , including the database schema, RLS, Auth, APIs, Edge Functions, and what  not  to put in Supabase.

prompt: What do you know about Supabase (@supabase on X/Twitter)?
answer:
Yes.
is one of the most important developer-platform companies in the current AI/startup ecosystem, and  @supabase on X  is its official developer-focused account.
What Supabase actually is
The simplest description is:
Supabase is a developer platform built around Postgres that gives you most of the backend you need to build an application.
Every Supabase project gets a full Postgres database, rather than a proprietary database abstraction. Around that database, Supabase provides:
• Postgres database  — relational data, SQL , extensions, indexes, triggers , etc.
• Authentication  — email/password, magic  links, OAuth/social  login, phone auth , etc.
• Row Level Security  (RLS)  — database-level authorization  policies.
• Storage  — files, images, videos , documents, with access  control.
• Realtime  — subscribe to database  changes and synchronize  state between clients .
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript /D eno functions.
• Auto-generated APIs  — REST APIs and  other ways of  interacting with your  database.
• Vector/AI capabilities  — including  pgvector  for embeddings.
• CLI, migrations, branching , local development and  self-hosting.
Supabase describes the  philosophy as making Postgres as easy  to use as  Firebase , while keeping the  underlying database accessible  and portable.
Why developers like it
The killer proposition is that you can go from:
"I have an idea" → "I have a working backend"
very quickly.
For example, suppose you're building a SaaS app. Instead of separately setting up:
Postgres + API server + auth provider + file storage + realtime infrastructure + serverless functions
you can start a Supabase project and get these pieces integrated.
That's particularly attractive for  AI-generated applications / "vibe coding."  AI coding tools can create a database schema, authentication, API calls and application logic without requiring the developer to manually assemble a traditional backend stack.
That trend has become a major growth engine for Supabase. In June 2026, TechCrunch reported that Supabase had nearly  10 million developers , with database launches up more than 600% year-over-year and more than 60% of new databases being launched by some kind of AI tool.
Why Postgres is such a big deal
This is probably the most important distinction between Supabase and something like Firebase.
Supabase isn't trying to hide the database from you.
You can use normal PostgreSQL:
CREATE TABLE customers (
You still have SQL, foreign keys, joins, indexes, transactions, extensions, functions, etc.
And you can directly use things such as  PostGIS  for geospatial data and  pgvector  for AI embeddings.
So Supabase is particularly attractive if you think:
"I want the simplicity of a managed backend, but I don't want to outgrow a proprietary database."
The AI angle is especially interesting
Supabase has increasingly positioned itself as infrastructure for the AI-native development ecosystem.
An AI application might look like:
LLM → Edge Function → Supabase/Postgres → pgvector → application
For example, you could store:
• users
• conversations
• documents
• embeddings
• permissions
• billing information
• application state
all inside Postgres .
The n an Edge  Function can call  an LLM, retrieve  relevant vectors, enforce  authentication, and return  the result to  your application. Supabase  explicitly documents Edge  Functions for things  like AI inference  and orchestrating calls  to external LLM  APIs.
Supabase also released @supabase/server  in public beta  in May 2026  to simplify authentication  and server-side  Supabase setup across  environments such as  Vercel Functions, Cloudflare  Workers, Hono, Bun  and Edge Functions .
And it's genuinely  open source
This is another  major part of  the brand.
Supabase says its  stack is open  source and designed  to be self -hostable.  Its architecture is  built from open -source components rather  than being a  completely proprietary  backend platform.
That gives it  a somewhat different  philosophy from many  "backend-as-a -service" products:
Firebase: Google-managed backend  with a proprietary  ecosystem.
Supabase: Managed service built  around open-source  technologies, with Postgres  at the center .
That's not quite  as simple as  saying "Supabase is  open-source Firebase "—Supabase itself explicitly  says it's  not a 1 :1 Firebase mapping .
The business has  become huge
This is one  of the more  remarkable parts of  the story.
