prompt: What do you know about Supabase (@supabase on X/Twitter)?
answer:
is one of the  more interesting developer-platform companies right now. The short version:  it’s essentially “Postgres + the batteries you normally have to build around it,” delivered as a developer-friendly platform.
What Supabase actually is
At its core, every Supabase project gives you a  real PostgreSQL database  rather than a proprietary database abstraction. Around that, Supabase provides:
• Postgres database  — SQL, relational modeling, extensions, indexes, etc.
• Authentication  — email /password, passwordless, OAuth and other identity providers.
• Storage  — object/file storage integrated with your database and Row Level Security.
• Realtime  — subscribe to database changes and synchronize state between clients.
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript functions running close  to users.
• Data APIs  — automatically generated APIs for your database.
• Vector/AI capabilities  — storing and searching embeddings using Postgres.
• Cron and Queues  — background/scheduled workloads.
That architecture is important. Rather than saying  “here's a database, now go assemble 8 other SaaS products,”  Supabase tries to make Postgres the center of the application stack.
Why developers like it
The big selling point is  Postgres without having to become a database-infrastructure expert .
For example, you can build a SaaS app with:
React/Next.js → Supabase Auth → Supabase API → PostgreSQL → Supabase Storage
and add Realtime or Edge Functions when needed.
The database is still ordinary Postgres, which is a major advantage over some backend-as-a-service products: you're not locked into an exotic database model. Supabase explicitly describes each project as a full Postgres database.
The other major attraction is  Row Level Security (RLS) . You can put authorization rules directly around database data, e.g. conceptually:
user A → can read rows belonging to user A
That makes Supabase particularly compelling for applications where permissions and relational data matter.
Supabase vs. Firebase
This is probably the most useful comparison.
Firebase  is historically Google’s backend platform centered around its own NoSQL database ecosystem.
Supabase  is centered around PostgreSQL.
So the philosophical difference is roughly:
Firebase → “Build your app on Google's managed backend primitives.”
Supabase → “Build your app on Postgres, and we'll provide the backend primitives around it.”
For developers who already know SQL, relational modeling, Postgres extensions, migrations, and database constraints, Supabase can feel much more natural.
The business is getting serious
Supabase is no longer just a cool open-source developer project.
It raised  $200 million in Series D at a $2 billion valuation in 2025 , and later raised  $100 million at a $5 billion valuation in 2025 , according to reporting summarized by Axios.
That jump is notable because it reflects how much investor interest has shifted toward the  AI application infrastructure  layer.
And Supabase is particularly well positioned there: AI-generated applications still need databases, authentication, file storage, APIs, permissions, background jobs, and vector search.
Supabase itself now explicitly positions the platform for AI builders and frameworks.
The @supabase X account
The account you're referring to,  @supabase , is the company's main developer/community presence on X. Its communication style is very developer-oriented: product launches, Postgres tips, demos, ecosystem projects, community activity, and occasionally the irreverent/meme-heavy style common among modern developer-tool companies.
That's actually part of Supabase's broader strategy:  they've built a strong developer brand , rather than presenting themselves as just another cloud database vendor.
How they make money
There's a free tier, then paid plans based on things like compute, database size, storage, egress, MAUs, Realtime usage and Edge Function invocations.
Currently, the  Pro plan starts at $25/month , while Team is $599/month and Enterprise is custom.
One thing worth understanding if you're evaluating Supabase commercially:  the database itself isn't necessarily the expensive part . Compute, egress, storage, Realtime connections/messages, and other usage can become meaningful as an application scales. Supabase's billing documentation lays out these usage-based components.
My take
I think Supabase is interesting because it sits at the intersection of  three very strong trends :
Postgres becoming the default application database.
Developers wanting integrated backend infrastructure instead of assembling dozens of services.
AI making it dramatically easier to create applications, increasing demand for simple backend infrastructure.
The particularly clever part is  Postgres as the foundation . They're not trying to invent an entirely new data model. They're taking something developers already trust and wrapping a modern developer experience around it.
So if you're asking  “Is Supabase just another Firebase clone?”  —  no, that's underselling it.  I'd describe it more accurately as a  Postgres-centric application platform that competes with pieces of Firebase, AWS, Vercel's backend ecosystem, Neon, and various standalone auth/storage/API providers.
And if you're interested in  Supabase specifically as a company/business/investment , there's a much more interesting story to unpack: its growth, $5B valuation, open-source strategy, AI positioning, competitive moat , and whether the economics of managed Postgres can support a truly huge company.

prompt: What do you know about https://supabase.com/ and @supabase on X/Twitter?
answer:
Yes. I looked at both the company and its X presence, including recent information, and  Supabase is much more than “Firebase but open source.”  It has become one of the important infrastructure companies in the current AI/app-building ecosystem.
What Supabase is
describes itself as  “the Postgres development platform.”  The core idea is straightforward:
Give developers a real PostgreSQL database, then build the surrounding backend infrastructure around it.
A Supabase project includes:
• Postgres database  — a full PostgreSQL database rather than a proprietary database abstraction.
• Authentication  — email/password, magic links, OTP, OAuth, SSO, etc.
• Row Level Security (RLS)  — database-level authorization policies.
• Storage  — files, images, videos, etc.
• Realtime  — subscribe to database changes and synchronize state.
• Edge Functions  — server-side TypeScript functions.
• Data APIs  — automatically generated REST/GraphQL APIs.
• Vector/AI capabilities  — including PostgreSQL extensions such as  pgvector .
The architectural choice that matters most is  Postgres at the center . Auth, APIs, Storage, Realtime, Functions, etc. are integrated around that database.
That's a pretty powerful proposition because PostgreSQL itself is extremely mature and portable.
Why developers like it
The big appeal is  how much backend you get without having to assemble it yourself .
For example, instead of building:
Postgres + API server + auth provider + object storage + WebSocket infrastructure + permissions system
you can start with one Supabase project.
And you're not locked into an exotic database. Supabase explicitly positions its Postgres databases as portable, and you can connect using ordinary PostgreSQL tooling.
This makes it particularly attractive for:
• SaaS applications
• MVPs and startups
• internal tools
• mobile apps
• AI applications
• marketplaces
• dashboards
• collaborative/realtime applications
• products being built rapidly with AI coding tools
The really interesting part: AI / “vibe coding”
This is where Supabase has experienced an enormous  acceleration.
AI coding tools can generate a frontend relatively easily, but they still need somewhere to put:
• users
• application data
• permissions
• files
• embeddings
• application state
• APIs
Supabase is almost tailor-made for this.
Recent reporting says Supabase had  nearly 10 million developers using the platform by June 2026 , with database launches growing more than 600% year-over-year and more than 60% of new databases reportedly being launched by some kind of AI tool.
That helps explain why you see Supabase repeatedly appearing alongside companies/tools such as  Lovable, Bolt, Replit, Figma and other AI-assisted development products .
And this isn't merely marketing positioning: Supabase has been building AI-oriented tooling around its platform as well.
The company itself has become quite valuable
The growth has been extraordinary.
According to TechCrunch:
• April 2025:  $200M Series D , ~$2B valuation
• October 2025 :  $100M Series E , ~$5B valuation
• June 2026:  $500M Series F , ~$10B pre-money valuation / ~$10.5B post-money
The June 2026 round reportedly brought total funding to roughly  $1 billion .
So we're no longer talking about a niche open-source developer project. Supabase has become a major venture-backed infrastructure company.
And what about @supabase on X?
The official account is
.
The account currently describes Supabase as  “The Postgres development platform”  and had roughly  202K followers  when I checked.
What's interesting about the account is its role in Supabase's developer-marketing strategy.
It isn't just corporate announcements. The account tends to mix:
• PostgreSQL  content
• product launches
• developer education
• open-source projects
• memes/humor
• AI/developer-tool discussions
• community projects
• integrations
• ecosystem announcements
For example, Supabase has used X to highlight PostgreSQL ecosystem work such as  pgvector , rather than treating Postgres merely as an implementation detail.
And its Supabase Wrapped 2025  post is a good example of how it uses social media to turn platform usage into community content.
The  strategic thing I'd pay attention to
If you're evaluating Supabase as a  company , rather than simply asking “is this a good database?”, I think the interesting thesis is:
Supabase sits at the intersection of three unusually strong trends:
PostgreSQL ↓ Cloud infrastructure becoming easier ↓ AI making software development dramatically cheaper/faster
AI can generate the application code, but applications still need a  persistent, structured, permissioned backend .
Supabase is positioning itself as that backend.
That's potentially much more significant than the “Firebase alternative” framing.
There is also an interesting second-order effect: as AI makes it possible for vastly more people to build software, the number of people who need a database increases. Supabase's CEO specifically credited AI tools such  as Claude Code and Codex with expanding the population of people who can build software.
One important caveat
Supabase's simplicity can also make it  easy to build something insecure .
RLS is extremely powerful, but developers need to actually write the correct policies. A Supabase database being configured with RLS doesn't automatically mean the application's authorization model is correct. Supabase itself emphasizes RLS as the mechanism for  safely exposing database access to applications.
That's becoming particularly relevant as AI-generated applications proliferate.
My short take
If I were explaining Supabase in one sentence:
Supabase is trying to make PostgreSQL the default programmable backend for the next generation of software—particularly software increasingly built by AI-assisted developers.
And  @supabase on X is a fairly important part of that strategy , because Supabase has built a strong developer/community brand rather than marketing itself like traditional enterprise infrastructure.
If you're asking because you're considering  Supabase for a project, evaluating the company as an investment/competitor, or trying to understand why @supabase has such a strong presence on X , I can go considerably deeper into that specific angle.

answer:
Yes.
is one of the more important developer platforms in the modern web/AI stack. In simple terms:
Supabase is “Postgres + everything you typically need around it,” delivered as a developer-friendly platform.
What Supabase actually is
The key architectural decision is that  PostgreSQL is the center of the product . Unlike Firebase, which is built around a proprietary NoSQL database model, Supabase gives every project a real Postgres database—you can use SQL, extensions, indexes, foreign keys, functions, triggers, etc.
Around that database, Supabase provides:
• Postgres database  — a full managed PostgreSQL database.
• Authentication  — email/password, passwordless login, OAuth/social providers, SSO, and increasingly passkeys.
• Row Level Security (RLS)  — PostgreSQL policies that let you define exactly which  rows a user can access.
• Storage  — object/file storage integrated with Postgres and RLS.
• Realtime  — database-change subscriptions, broadcasts, and presence/state synchronization.
• Edge Functions  —  server-side TypeScript/Deno functions for APIs, webhooks, integrations, AI calls, etc.
• Data APIs  — automatically generated REST APIs and GraphQL support.
• Vector/AI capabilities  — storage and querying of  embeddings, plus integrations with AI tooling.
• Cron and Queues  — infrastructure for scheduled and asynchronous work.
• CLI/local development/self-hosting  — a major  part of the open-source philosophy.
So a typical application might look like:
Your application
The interesting thing is that these aren't isolated products glued together.  They share the same Postgres foundation.  Supabase's own architecture describes Auth, Storage, Realtime, Functions, APIs, and other services sitting around a project's Postgres instance.
Why developers like it
The biggest attraction is  how much backend you get without building it yourself .
Imagine you're building a SaaS application. Traditionally you'd need:
• PostgreSQL
• a database hosting provider
• an authentication system
• an API layer
• authorization
• file storage
• image/file serving
• realtime infrastructure
• serverless functions
• database backups
• migrations
• monitoring
• connection pooling
Supabase packages much of that together.
And because the underlying database is actual Postgres, you aren't forced into an artificial database abstraction. You can drop down into SQL whenever you want.
That's an unusually powerful combination of  Firebase-like developer experience + traditional relational database capabilities .
RLS is particularly important
One of Supabase's killer features is  Postgres Row Level Security .
For example, you might have:
projects
and tell Postgres:
A logged-in user can only read projects where  owner_id = their user ID .
That authorization rule lives at the database level rather than merely being an  if  statement in your frontend.
This is extremely useful for multi-tenant SaaS applications because the database itself enforces the boundary. Supabase explicitly recommends protecting tables exposed through its APIs with RLS.
The flip side is that  RLS is powerful enough to be dangerous if you don't understand it . Poorly designed policies can accidentally expose data—or make legitimate queries mysteriously return nothing.
Supabase and AI
This is one of the areas where Supabase has become particularly interesting.
Postgres makes a natural foundation for AI applications because you can keep:
Users
in one relational system.
Supabase supports vector embeddings and vector search, so you can build things like:
• RAG applications
• semantic search
• document Q&A
• recommendation systems
• AI agents with persistent memory
• hybrid keyword + semantic search
without introducing an entirely separate vector database for many workloads.
And Edge Functions can orchestrate calls to external AI models. Supabase specifically documents patterns for OpenAI and other AI integrations.
That makes it a very natural backend for the current generation of AI-first applications.

Supabase itself is careful to say it isn't simply a 1:1 Firebase clone—the underlying philosophy is different because it builds around open-source technologies and Postgres.
Is it actually open source?
This is an important distinction.
Yes, Supabase is genuinely open source in a meaningful way.  Its dashboard and major infrastructure components are built in the open, and Supabase supports self-hosting.
That doesn't mean  every service you interact with on Supabase's hosted platform is magically equivalent to running the entire production service yourself . There is still a commercial hosted platform, with operational conveniences and managed infrastructure.
But compared with many modern "developer platforms," the ability to inspect the source and self-host is a substantial difference.
Edge Functions
Supabase Edge Functions are another useful piece.
They're  TypeScript functions running on a Deno-compatible edge runtime , and they're particularly suited to short-lived backend operations such as:
• authenticated APIs
• Stripe webhooks
• GitHub webhooks
• AI requests
• email sending
• image generation
• integrations with third-party APIs
They can interact directly with your Supabase Auth, database, and Storage.
One important caveat: they're not a replacement for arbitrary long-running backend workers. Supabase itself recommends moving heavy, long-running jobs to background workers.
Where I think Supabase is strongest
I'd particularly consider it for:
• SaaS products
• AI applications
• Internal tools
• Mobile apps
• MVPs that might become serious products
• Multi-tenant applications
• Apps requiring relational data
• Applications where you want SQL
• Real-time collaborative products
• Developer tools
It's especially compelling if your stack is something like:
Next.js / React + TypeScript + Supabase + Vercel
or:
React Native / Expo + Supabase
because you can get from an empty repository to a functioning application surprisingly quickly.
Where I'd be more cautious
Supabase isn't automatically the right answer for every backend.
I'd think twice if you need:
• extremely specialized database infrastructure
• huge-scale distributed database workloads with unusual requirements
• very long-running background processing
• complex enterprise integration infrastructure
• extremely sophisticated event-stream processing
• infrastructure that must be entirely controlled inside your own environment
And there's a broader issue:  Supabase makes the easy path very easy, which can encourage people to build production systems without understanding Postgres, RLS, networking, connection pooling, indexes, migrations, or security.
You can absolutely build a serious production system on it—but understanding what's happening underneath becomes increasingly important as the application grows.
And the company itself is significant
Supabase has grown far beyond being a little Firebase alternative.
In October 2025 it announced a  $100M Series E at a $5B pre-money valuation . Then in June 2026, it announced a  $500M Series F at a $10B pre-money valuation , led by GIC.
The  2026 round is particularly interesting because Supabase is increasingly positioning itself not merely as a hosted application backend, but as a company investing heavily in  Postgres infrastructure itself . It simultaneously  announced  Multigres , an open-source project intended to make Postgres easier to scale horizontally, with sharding, pooling, failover and backup orchestration.
That's  a pretty strong signal about where the company sees its future.
My short take
If I had to reduce Supabase to one sentence:
Supabase is an open-source, developer-friendly application platform built around real PostgreSQL, combining database, authentication, authorization, storage, realtime, APIs, serverless functions, and increasingly AI infrastructure.
And  the Postgres decision is the key . That's what differenti ates Supabase from Firebase and many newer backend-as-a-service products.
If you're evaluating Supabase for  a specific project , I can also break down the architecture I'd recommend—including  Supabase vs Firebase vs Convex vs Neon vs a custom Postgres backend , and where I would  not  use Supabase.
